en: A Direct Explanation of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhatoṭara of Kasmīra during the Tang Dynasty;
explained by the Recluse Deqing of Mount Kuang, Hamsan, Ming Dynasty.
Preface by Cheng Mengyang Juewo of Xin’an:
This sutra takes the single dharma as its name; the one true dharmadhātu, the Tathāgata-garbha mind, as its essence;
the aspect of perfect illuminating awareness as its principle; the departure from delusion and realization of truth as its function; and the complete and sudden One Vehicle as its teaching.
Regarding the characteristic of naming by means of a single dharma, the treatise states: "That which is called 'dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.
The two characters *yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment) directly point to this one mind as the essence of the dharma-body. It has many designations:

it is also called Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahāparipūrṇabodhi*), also called the Wondrously Enlightened Luminous Mind (*prabhāsvara-citta*), also called the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-satya-dharmadhātu*), and also termed the Pure Tathāgatagarbha.

The pure true mind. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* refers to it as the "quiescent single mind," which is precisely what the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* calls the essence of the great universal dharma-gate of the one dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*).
Although there are many designations, they all refer to the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment; it is solely this single mind.
It is the fundamental basis for the causes and effects of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the delusion and awakening of ordinary beings and sages within the ten dharma realms.
It is the original source of all Buddhas, designated as the *dharmakāya*. It is the ground of the mind of all sentient beings, and is therefore named "Buddha-nature. All dharmas [arise from it].
Because all things are established based upon this mind, it is designated simply by the name "Dharma.

Its terms "Great," "Vast," and "Extensive" (Mahāvaipulya) signify the three great meanings of essence, attributes, and function inherent in this mental dharma. Among these, "Great" refers to the greatness of essence (*tathatā-mahattva*), meaning this single mind.

It encompasses the Dharma-realm with something remaining beyond; it expands into the great void without exterior. Transversally inclusive and vertically pervasive, it is "Great" because it is vast and has no outside.

"Square" (fang) refers to the magnitude of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, "square" is glossed as "Dharma" (*dharma*), meaning that this single mind is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Because of the existence of this nature-principle (*dharmatā*), upon hearing of the Buddha-nature even once, one is immediately able to give rise to understanding.
Circulating through long kalpas, it is maintained without loss; hence it is said that it serves as a model for things and gives rise to understanding.
It sustains its own nature by taking the formless true mind as the phenomenal principle; this is precisely what constitutes the greatness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*).

"Extensive" refers to the greatness of function (*kāritra-mahattva*), because it accords with the essence of this mind which is all-pervasive and leaves nothing out—there is no land where it does not appear, and no thing to which it does not extend.
Therefore, it is used as the "Great" [Vehicle]. This dharma-meaning is fully perfected within the one mind.

Within this sutra, this very mind is directly pointed out as the fundamental basis for the arising of Buddhas and the delusion or awakening of sentient beings, as well as for cultivation and realization; thus, it is said that the title is based on a single dharma.
*Sūtra* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Kie-king" (契經, *kīya-sūtra*). This is because all sutras spoken by the Buddha are collectively termed thus.

"Sūtra" (Kie-king) refers to a teaching that accords with both principle and the capacity of the audience. However, depending on whether it accords with the specific capacity of the listener, there are Great and Small [vehicles].
Those taught for the sake of followers of the Small Vehicle are called *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras;

those taught for the sake of followers of the Great Vehicle are called *nītārtha* (definitive) sūtras, meaning they reveal the ultimate, final discourse. Since the title here generally indicates this particular scripture, it is the definitive one among the Sūtra Piṭaka.

This is a definitive sūtra (*nītārtha-sūtra*), not one of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). The first ten characters represent the doctrinal principles (*dharma-artha*) elucidated by this single sūtra;
the subsequent character "sūtra" specifically points to the words and letters of this particular scripture that serve as the means of expression.

Regarding its essence being the True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*) or the Tathāgata-garbha mind, the sūtra states: "Entering the Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā-mahā-avabhāsa-garbha*)," which is...
The essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, the pure mind, is equal and non-dual; therefore, it is called "One True.
It is further said that its nature is ultimately perfect and complete like the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); this is termed the practice of the Dharma on the ground of cultivation (bhūmi).

It is first designated as the "Great Dharani Gate," which is the essence of the Great Universal Characteristic Dharma-gate of the single Dharma-realm, serving as the Bodhi of all Buddhas on the ground of cultivation.

Because it constitutes the fundamental basis of the Bodhisattva’s practice, this serves as the structural core of the entire sutra. Regarding its taking the "characteristic of perfect illumination and awakening" as its central tenet (*zong*):
the Sutra states, "The original ground of all Tathāgatas’ initial cultivation all relies upon the characteristic of pure, perfectly illuminating awakening;
only by permanently severing ignorance does one then achieve the Buddha-way. Therefore, this is established as the central tenet of the entire sutra. It is free from delusion...
Regarding "realizing the truth as its function," the Sūtra says: "Knowing these to be flowers in the sky, there is no further transmigration.
It also says: "Knowing illusion, one is immediately detached from it; being detached from illusion, one is awakened. Therefore, this is taken as its function.

Regarding "the One Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden as its doctrinal aspect," this is because this Sūtra exclusively discusses the nature of awakening, perfectly cultivates the three contemplations, and suddenly realizes the one mind. Although two [aspects] are listed...

The fifteen wheels are merely the transformation of a single mind; because there are no stages or sequential gradations, they take the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) as their doctrinal characteristic (*śāstralakṣaṇa*).
Nevertheless, these five layers constitute the methodological rule for Tiantai’s exegesis of the sutras, as they encompass the essential purport of the entire scripture.
Thus, when a student opens this volume, understanding this point means that half of the Master’s kindness has already been received.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhataira of Jibin during the Tang Dynasty.
This refers to the name and lineage of the translator. Jibin is the name of a kingdom in the Western Regions;

it is translated here as "Base Lineage" (*jianshong*), because when this country was first settled, low-born people established themselves as its sovereigns, and thus the name was handed down traditionally. Buddha... [The text ends here.]

"Jue" (覺) means "Awakening" in Chinese; "Tara" (多羅) means "Rescuer" (救) in Chinese. These are the names of the translators. The dates of their translations are recorded in detail in separate biographies.
This is the direct commentary by the Chan Master Deqing of Mount Huangan, who lived as a recluse on Mount Kuang.
The initial introduction.

From "Thus have I heard at one time" down to "the assembly of the Dharma of equality," this is collectively named the *Saddharmapratisaṃvid-avatāra-nidāna* (the Introduction of Certification and Faith). This is because the beginning of all sūtras invariably contains [this formula].
This introduction is called the "General Preface" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*). It establishes the testimony that the Dharma was transmitted through the Buddha’s final instructions as requested by Ānanda.

Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard": this means that when Ānanda compiled the treasury of the Dharma (*dharmapiṭaka*), he orally proclaimed the Buddha’s words, stating, "Such is this Dharma; I, Ānanda, heard it from the Buddha; it is not a fabrication. At one time...
These words have no fixed reference; they simply indicate the time when the Buddha and his disciples gathered through the convergence of their spiritual resonance.
Therefore, whenever a sutra is preached, it is said to be "at one time."
*Bhagavān* is also called *Bhagavat*.
This is merely a difference between the "archaic" (*chū*) and "modern" (*xià*) pronunciations of the Sanskrit sound. It is a title for the fruit of Buddhahood.
This title has never been translated [into Chinese], because it contains many meanings and thus is not translated. That is to say, this single term possesses six meanings. First:
1. Sovereignty (vaśitā), 2. Radiance (tejas), 3. Dignity (saumyatā), 4. Renown (yaśas), 5. Auspiciousness (śrī), and 6. Nobility (māhātmya). These all designate the virtues of a Buddha.
If one were to translate even a single name, it would fail to encompass the full range of meanings; therefore, the Sanskrit term alone is retained.
This is an example of one of the five reasons for not translating. He is the master who expounds the Dharma.

He entered the Great Treasury of Radiant Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā-mahā-avabhāsa-garbha*), where he dwelt in the correct reception of samādhi, sustained by the light-adorned empowerment of all Tathāgatas;

this is the place where the sutra was preached. The Buddha has three bodies, namely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body; correspondingly, there are also three lands upon which they rely.

These are the *Sāmbhogika-kāya* (Enjoyment Body), the *Nirmāṇa-kāya* (Transformation Body), and the *Upāya-śeṣa* (Residual Means) lands. Regarding the dharmas, the Buddha of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) relies upon the *Tathatā-prabhāsvara-kṣetra* (Land of Quiescent Light).

The *Sāmbhogika-kāya* Buddha relies upon the *Pratipūrṇa-vipāka-alaṃkāra-kṣetra* (Land of Real Reward Adornment); this is Vairocana Buddha, who dwells in the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha-loka-dhātu*) and teaches the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The *Nirmāṇa-kāya*, namely Śākyamuni Buddha, relies upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the city of Śrāvastī in the human realm.
In places such as monasteries, he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for the sake of humans, devas, and others.

As for the place where this sutra is now being preached, it is called the "Treasury of Great Supernatural Powers and Radiance" (*mahā-ṛddhi-prabhā-garbha*); this is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā-kṣetra*), which is the locus of the Dharmakāya.

Regarding the term *samādhi*, this is translated as "Right Concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). "Right Reception" (*samyak-saṃvedana*) refers to the experience within that Right Concentration; this indicates that this sutra pertains to the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya.
The right concentration and right meditative absorption taught by the Buddha of identical essence is the place where one personally experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "the abiding maintenance of the light-adornment of all Tathāgatas," this refers to the land of *dharmatā*. It is the land of eternal, quiescent light realized by all Buddhas;
it is adorned with light, not with other precious objects. This land of quiescent light is the *dharmatā*...
It is the secure dwelling of the body; hence it is called "abiding and maintaining. This teaching, being based upon the Truth (*tathatā*), cannot be compared to other Buddhas or other locations;
it reveals that the Dharma is most preeminent.
This is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings.
What is called "tranquil light" (jigō) is the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) wherein the birth and buddhahood of beings are equal;

it is the peaceful dwelling of all Buddhas, which is precisely the ground of non-deluded awakening inherently possessed by sentient beings. This reveals the true realm in which the real and the delusive are non-dual.
Furthermore,
the fundamental limit of the quiescent equality of body and mind is perfectly fulfilled throughout the ten directions and accords with non-duality;
this refers to the true realm of the serene light, wherein both the bodies and minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings are equally quiescent and extinguished.
The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of equality—this refers to the profundity of its essence. "Fulfilling the ten directions"—this refers to the vastness of its function.

To say that its function is fulfilled means it encompasses the ten directions; it is so vast that there is nothing outside of it. "Non-dual conformity" is a textual inversion; it should read "conforming to non-duality.
This means that all sages and ordinary beings alike return to this single, equal limit within it; therefore, it is so called.
It accords with non-duality.
Within the realm of non-duality, it manifests all pure lands.
This supreme realm of non-duality is the ground where all Buddhas personally experience the bliss of the Dharma. Because it is devoid of body and mind—

Regarding the marks (*lakṣaṇa*): how could there be a distinction between principal and attendant? If there were no principal and attendant, there would be no speaking and no demonstrating; thus, the activity of teaching the Dharma would not exist.
Now, when it is said that "various pure lands manifest from the non-dual realm," this precisely reveals that the other-enjoyment land (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) manifests from the self-enjoyment [land].
This is the reward land (*vipākabhūmi*) where the Dharma of self-nature is taught for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).

Within this [state], there is indeed speaking and listening. However, although there is speaking and listening in this land, the Tathāgata still remains in samādhi and has never emerged from meditative concentration.

How, then, can there be speaking? This is intended to reveal that this sutra is the Dharma spoken by the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, manifesting the state that transcends the realms of mind, thought, and consciousness. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s most...

This *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is exceptionally pure and cannot be compared to other sutras. In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the Dharma-body preaches the Dharma, thereby attesting to the Buddha through the Dharma;
this sutra attests to the Buddha through the locus. When these two sutras are viewed together, they truly possess a profound underlying meaning.
This is something that has never been understood before; please contemplate it deeply.
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, among whom were the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and others.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva,
Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva, Vaśitāprāpta Bodhisattva, Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva,
Samantabodhi Bodhisattva, Pariniṣpannabodhi Bodhisattva, Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva, and others, who served as the leaders, together with their retinues.
All have entered samādhi and dwell together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.

This indicates the names of the leaders among the retinue of attendants. Regarding the twelve great beings (*mahāsattvas*), the traditional commentaries all explain their names by means of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
However, as each possesses its own specific virtue, there is likely no need to be so strictly bound [to that interpretation]. As for the statement "all have entered samādhi":

Since the Buddha is the retributive form (vipākābha) of the Dharma-body itself, and the land is the retributive land (vipākabhūmi) of the Land of Quiescent Light (jigguang), how could there be any listeners with distracted minds when the Buddha himself has entered samādhi to preach the Dharma of self-nature?
Therefore, one must enter samādhi before one can dwell together in this assembly of the equal Dharma. Question: [Regarding] the principal and the associates...
"If all are in samādhi, then there is no hearing. By what means, then, can the Dharma be manifested? He replied:

"This is the wondrous Dharma of the inconceivable. Long ago, when Śāriputra sat in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave, Śakra, Lord of Devas, scattered flowers and praised him, saying he had well expounded the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra said: 'In truth, I have said nothing. Śakra said: 'Venerable One, you have expounded it by means of non-expounding.'"

I listen with a listening that transcends hearing; such is the way one listens to this true Prajñā. Having understood this, one may properly speak and properly listen within the Samādhi of Trustworthiness.
It is said that since a Bodhisattva possesses the formal etiquette of making a request, there must necessarily be a textual passage concerning their entering and departing [the samādhi].
Perhaps the translator omitted it, but such an interpretation is overly restrictive. Have you not heard that the Nāga is always in a state of meditative composure?
He is always in meditative concentration; there is no time when he is not in concentration. How could it be that only the Buddha is constantly in concentration while the bodhisattvas are not?
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage manifest the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi to deliver sentient beings—how could they emerge from concentration?

If one insists that they must emerge from concentration in order to listen to and receive requests for instruction, then one would contradict the teaching that "without arising from the extinction-concentration, one manifests various majestic demeanors."
[This] ritual procedure—how could it not be the concern of a bodhisattva? Taking this opportunity, let students take note of it.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that you will, for the sake of all the members of the Dharma assembly who have gathered for this convention, speak of the Tathāgata’s original arising in purity. [Note: This passage describes the majestic deportment of the questioner as arranged by the author of the sutra.
Regarding the practice of the dharmas of the causal stage and all bodhisattvas within the Mahāyāna, they give rise to a pure mind and remain far removed from all ailments;
they are able to ensure that sentient beings of future末 (mò) kalpas who seek the Mahāyāna do not fall into wrong views.
This is the formal request for instruction. The inquiry contains two intentions:
first, to ask by what dharmas the Tathāgata relied upon and what practices he cultivated while on the bodhisattva path to attain buddhahood;
second, to ask how present-day bodhisattvas—who have already generated the pure aspiration within the Mahāyāna to attain buddhahood and deliver sentient beings—should proceed in practice.
Cultivating the mind through practice, one attains right knowledge and vision, and does not fall into the malady of partiality or deviation.

If you grant us this instruction, then those sentient beings of future末 (mò) ages who give rise to the Mahāyāna mind will, by practicing according to what is taught today, avoid falling into false views.
Although this question was asked for the sake of the present, it is in fact primarily for [the sake of] the future.
"This is the mind of compassionate vow directed toward those with the potential of the future.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. He made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
This describes the earnest sincerity with which they seek the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practice of the Dharma on the causal ground, as well as for the sake of those in the final age..."
"All sentient beings who seek the Mahāyāna shall attain correct sustenance and not fall into false views. Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you.
This is the praise of the excellent inquiry, the exhortation to listen, and the permission to speak; hereafter, follow this same pattern.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, together with the great assembly, listened in silence.
This indicates that they welcomed the sound of the Dharma with delight and waited in contemplation to hear it; the following sections are modeled after this.
The protocols for the twelve great beings requesting the Dharma are identical in each instance, and as the text is most orderly, it is not explained again.
"Good son, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
From it flow forth all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*. It instructs the bodhisattvas.
The original ground of practice for all Tathāgatas relies entirely upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating pure enlightenment; only by permanently severing ignorance does one become a Buddha."

This directly indicates the fundamental ground of origination. In the Tathāgata’s ground of practice, the single dharma of Perfect Enlightenment (Caryā-bodhi) alone is designated as the root of cultivation.
Now, regarding the designation of this Perfect Enlightenment as the "Gate of Dhāraṇī": *dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term.
This is called "total retention" (dhāraṇī). It means to encompass all phenomena and to maintain immeasurable meanings.

Taking this Perfect Enlightenment as the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the ten dharma-realms, all holy ones and ordinary beings, the environment and its inhabitants, delusion and awakening, cause and effect—all are established based upon this single mind of Perfect Enlightenment. Since there is not a single dharma that does not possess it, it is so named.

In summary, because cause and effect are preserved without the slightest loss or destruction, it is called "retaining" (*dhāraṇī*). Because all holy ones and ordinary beings pass through it without exception, it is termed a "gate.
As for "flowing forth," this refers to the meaning of being established by means of this [gate]. Now, regarding this essence of awakening:
It is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and the ground of the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of all sentient beings. Although it is defiled, it remains undefiled;
therefore, it is called "pure. Since from the beginning it has never been false or subject to change, it is termed "True Suchness" (*tathatā*).

It merely fails to manifest because it is obscured by ignorance. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas, while on the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), rely upon this true mind of fundamental awakening to give rise to their initial resolve.
The wisdom of awakening exhausts ignorance; when the beginning and the fundamental merge as one, it is called ultimate awakening.
Having attained the fruit of Bodhi, returning to the quiescent single mind is termed "perfect stillness" (*parinirvāṇa*), which is called *nirvāṇa*.

Thus, one knows that the resultant virtues of all Buddhas are established based upon this single mind of perfect awakening; therefore, it is said that they "flow forth" from it. However, it is not only...
The fruit of Buddhahood, as well as the various *pāramitās* practiced on the causal ground of a Bodhisattva, likewise emerge from this;
hence the word "and. Since the causal ground of all Buddhas constitutes the fundamental basis for the conduct of a Bodhisattva, it is called "instruction.

Therefore, there is no other dharma for the causal ground from which all Tathāgatas originally arose upon attaining Buddhahood; they all rely upon this Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*).
The luminosity of self-nature shines back upon the tranquil and pure essence of awakening; appearance is identical to the essence of nature.
When this perfect illumination penetrates everything without exception, ignorance is forever severed and the Dharmakāya is fully realized;
there is only this single dharma. Therefore it is said: "All depend upon the perfectly illuminating aspect of pure awakening to forever sever ignorance. Only then...
This is the attainment of Buddhahood. Now, "perfect illumination" is the wisdom of the three contemplations within one mind;
"the aspect of pure awakening" is the essence of the three truths within one mind. The entire sutra merely elucidates this single phrase. A question is asked:

This passage from the *Cloud* [Sutra], which states, "There is a great dharani-gate named Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue), from which all things flow forth," and so on, appears similar in its phrasing to that of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states, "There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King," and so on.
What is the difference in their meaning? Answer: Although the phrasing is similar, there is a slight difference in meaning. This is because...
The Sūtra directly points to the essence of awakening as the mind for the causal ground (*nidāna-citta*).
That sūtra takes the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama as the expedient means for the initial aspiration to attain Buddhahood.

While these differ in terms of essence and function, what they share in common is that the sūtra first establishes the non-arising and non-perishing mind as the fundamental cause of cultivation, and based upon it, constructs the Great Śūraṅgama [Samādhi].

Samādhi. However, the mind that is neither born nor extinguished is precisely this essence of awakening. That "Samādhi Adorned at the Head" is precisely this aspect of pure, perfect illumination of awakening.

Since this perfect illumination is that Great Samādhi, and the aspect of awakening herein is that mind which is neither born nor extinguished, when function is subsumed within the essence, they are ultimately non-dual. Therefore, both constitute the foundation for attaining Buddhahood. Question:
It says: "The Buddha stated that the Dharani-gate of Perfect Enlightenment is the ground for the Tathagata’s original arising.

It further states that pure True Suchness is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings which is non-deluded. It also states that all are based upon the aspect of the perfectly illuminating, pure awakening;
thus, fundamentally there is no ignorance to be severed. Suddenly it says: "Only by eternally severing ignorance..."
If one attains the Way of Buddhahood, then these meanings do not overlap. I venture to ask for their essential purport. He replied: "This meaning is profound and subtle;

it cannot be grasped by a coarse mind. Please allow me to explain it tentatively. Thus, the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment is the Dharmakāya, which is equal and non-dual for both Buddhas and sentient beings.
When this Dharmakāya transmigrates through the five paths of existence, it is termed 'sentient beings.'"
However, pure *tathatā* (suchness) is the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and the *buddhatva* (Buddha-nature) of all sentient beings.

It is precisely because of the initial single thought of ignorance and non-awakening that one becomes deluded regarding this *dharmakāya*, thereby forming the illusory and false body and mind of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Thus, while the originally present *pūrṇajñāna* (perfect enlightenment) constitutes the non-deluded Buddha-nature, it cannot be defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said that purity is fundamentally non-delusory and unchanging; hence, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).

Thus, the single phrase "pure *tathatā*" points directly to the Buddha-nature within the delusion of sentient beings. This is because all Buddhas, while on the stage of practice (*bhūmi*), were likewise sentient beings;
they merely relied upon the Buddha-nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) to give rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) and exhaustively sever all afflictions.
Illumination (*vidyā*). When the beginning and the source are unified, it is called the attainment of *bodhi*. Returning to realize the quiescent single mind, it is therefore called *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the fruits and virtues of the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas are all obtained only after returning from delusion to awakening through cultivation.
Therefore, it is said: "Only by eternally severing ignorance does one become a Buddha. Now, the methods for cultivation and severance are all based on the Perfect [Teaching].
The wisdom-light of the self-nature’s awakening shines back upon the essence of the mind, which is quiescent and pure; therefore, it is called the "perfectly illuminating aspect of pure awakening.
When the radiance of the self-nature shines forth once, ignorance is suddenly shattered; therefore, it is called "permanently severed.
This is truly the secret key to attaining Buddhahood, the wondrous gateway for sudden enlightenment and sudden realization, serving as the cause for the Tathāgata.
Regarding the "Dharma-practice of the Grounds," this sutra directly points to the essential meaning of the perfect and sudden One Mind;

therefore, it is presented at the outset as the fundamental purport of the entire scripture. Its words and meanings are profound and subtle, not to be understood by those of shallow knowledge; thus, they are here specifically elucidated.
"What is ignorance?
This question seeks to explain the essence of ignorance, intending to reveal the power of its perfect illumination. The following provides the explanation:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions, like a person who has lost their way."
Now, shifting the context: you falsely identify the four elements as the characteristics of your own body, and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of your own mind.
This is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky or a second moon.
This explains the root of ignorance. It means that sentient beings inherently possess the *dharmakāya* and originally have no birth or death.
Now, due to the ignorance of the first moment of non-awakening, they are deluded regarding their original Buddha-nature.
They give rise to greed, anger, and delusion, create various karmas, and falsely grasp at the birth and death of the six realms; therefore, it is called "various inversions. Although...

While circulating through birth and death, the Dharma-body remains profoundly still and unmoving; it is like a person who has lost their sense of direction, while the directions themselves have not actually shifted.

The reason for this delusion is that one turns one's back on the Dharma-body and merely identifies with the illusory body—a provisional union of the four elements—as one’s own self, falsely grasping at the shadows of the six sense objects and engaging in discursive thoughts and conceptualizations.
This mind is the true mind. It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. The diseased eyes are a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*);
the flowers in the sky are a metaphor for the illusory body; and the second moon is a metaphor for the illusory mind. Because one clings to the illusory and loses the real, it is called "inversion."
"Good son, empty space is truly without flowers; it is the sick person who grasps at them through delusion.

Because of this deluded grasping, they are not only confused about the intrinsic nature of this empty space, but are also deluded regarding the actual place where the flowers arise. Due to this false existence, they revolve in birth and death;
therefore, it is called ignorance."
This analogy illustrates the essence of ignorance. It means that the Dharmakāya is fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, just as space is fundamentally devoid of flowers.
Now, to falsely identify the four elements as a body is like grasping at illusory flowers in the sky as being truly existent.

Because of this false attachment, one is not only deluded regarding the fundamental Dharmakāya; thus it is said that one is "confused about the self-nature of this empty space," and furthermore, one also...
One knows that this delusory body arises from ignorance; therefore, it is said that one is deluded regarding the place where those real flowers grow.
Because of this inversion, there is the cycle of birth and death. This is the very essence of ignorance.
Good son, this ignorance has no real substance. It is like a person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not non-existent;
yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found. It is like various empty flowers that vanish into space; one cannot say there is a specific place where they are extinguished.
Why? Because there is no place of birth. All sentient beings, within that which is unborn, falsely perceive it as such.
There is arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called "revolving in birth and death.
This explanation clarifies that the essence of ignorance is empty, thereby demonstrating that birth and death have never existed from the very beginning.

Since birth and death are merely inverted perceptions within delusion—like events in a dream that become empty upon awakening—they are fundamentally non-arising. Thus, because birth is originally without birth, [it is empty].

Because even cessation itself has no cessation. Just as flowers in the sky have no fixed place of extinction, so too, son of good family, when a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, he knows these to be like flowers in the sky;

thus there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death. It is not that they are absent because of some deliberate act; rather, they are absent by their very nature.
This directly reveals the wondrous gate of sudden enlightenment and manifests the power of perfect illumination; it is expressed solely by the single character "knowing" (zhi).

This means that when the Buddhas practiced on the causal ground, they relied solely on the luminosity of the self-nature of perfect awakening to perfectly illuminate the tranquil, extinguished essence of their own minds.
In a single thought-moment, they fully realized that the body, mind, and world are like flowers in the sky—primordially non-existent.
Then birth and death are severed instantaneously in the present moment. Because body and mind are fundamentally empty, there is no one who can undergo birth and death.
This is not something that becomes non-existent after being produced; it is simply because the original self-nature has always been non-existent from the very beginning.
That cognizer is like empty space. That which knows empty space is itself the appearance of flowers in the sky. Furthermore, one cannot say that the nature of cognition is non-existent;
both existence and non-existence are discarded. This is what is called "conformity with pure awakening."

This brushing away eliminates the traces of the opposition between subject and object, thereby revealing the wisdom of the ultimate single mind—perfectly illuminating, equal, and quiescent pure awakening.
When it says "that which cognizes," it refers to the aforementioned cognition that [knows] these are flowers in the sky;
this is what is called "perfect illumination. It is the light of wisdom inherently possessed by the self-nature, serving as the wisdom that performs the act of illuminating.
The character "zhě" (者) refers to the object illuminated, which is the mark of pure awakening.

Just as empty space serves as a metaphor for the essence of awakening that performs the illumination—namely, the so-called Pure Dharmakāya, which is like empty space—it is said that although this essence of awakening is inherently present, it was previously obscured by ignorance and thus remained unawakened from the beginning.
Now, by relying on the single illumination of the light of wisdom...
Then ignorance is suddenly shattered, and the fundamental substance manifests immediately. Thus, the birth and death of kalpas are severed all at once.
This is what is meant by "knowing these are but flowers in the sky, and there is no more wandering in saṃsāra. This specifically demonstrates that the illumination of wisdom is efficacious.
Regarding the phrase "one who knows empty space," the word "this" (*cǐ*) refers back to the aforementioned illuminating wisdom; the meaning is that, first, by means of...

Wisdom illuminates delusion; when delusion is extinguished, wisdom likewise ceases to exist. Since that which is illuminated is already quiescent, if one retains the cognition that performs the illumination, this is still ignorance;
therefore, it must be discarded. Thus it is said: "One who knows empty space perceives the marks of flowers in the sky.

This means that both subject and object are forgotten, and quiescence and illumination are non-dual. Upon reaching this state, there is only suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*), the essence of illumination itself.
It stands independently; therefore, it is said that its nature of non-cognition cannot be said not to exist.

Only when mind and objects are both forgotten and subject and object are both extinguished can it be said that both existence and non-existence are discarded. In this way, one accords with the quiescent single mind;
therefore, it is said: "This is what is called 'conforming to pure awakening'. This passage is inverted; it should read "conforming to pure awakening," which refers to what was mentioned previously.
It is said that this accords with non-duality.
Why? Because it is the nature of empty space; because it is eternally unmoving; because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing; because there is neither cognition nor vision;
and because, like the nature of the Dharmadhātu, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions. This is what is called the cause.

The "Dharma-practice of the Ground" (*bhūmi-dharmācāra*) investigates and explains the essence of the mind that is tranquil and extinguished (*śānta-nirvṛta-citta-svabhāva*), further manifesting the absolute, non-referential true mind (*atyanta-anapekṣa-bhūta-citta*) to demonstrate the characteristic of pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodha-lakṣaṇa*).
Why is it necessary to repeatedly negate and sweep away both subject and object? Because the essence of the tranquil and extinguished mind is fundamentally...
Its coming is like the nature of empty space: eternally abiding and immovable; this reveals emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That is to say, although there currently exist body, mind, birth, and death, they are fundamentally like flowers in the sky, because within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is neither arising nor ceasing, and it admits of no cognition or perception;
this reveals the conventional (*prajñapti*). "Like" (*yathā*) means "in accordance with"; that is to say, it accords with the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, reaching its ultimate limit.
It is perfected, for it pervades the ten directions; this reveals the center. This is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the truly wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind.
On the stage of the causal ground, the Tathāgata has nothing other than this.
By means of this, Bodhisattvas give rise to a pure mind within the Mahāyāna. Sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this will not fall into false views.

When a bodhisattva resolves their mind, it should do so by means of this; thus, this constitutes the true cause. When sentient beings practice in reliance upon this, it constitutes the correct practice;
therefore, they do not fall into false views. This concludes the purport of the question and answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Mañjuśrī, you should know: All Tathāgatas, from their original ground of practice, Awakened through wisdom and realized The nature of ignorance; They know it to be like flowers in the sky."
One is thus able to escape the cycle of transmigration. Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream:

upon waking, the dreamer cannot be found, for the awakened state is like space—equanimous, unmoving, and unchanging. When awakening pervades the ten directions, one immediately attains the Way of the Buddha;
yet when all illusions have ceased, there is no place to be found, and even the attainment of the Way is non-existent.
Because its nature is inherently perfect, within this, the Bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta.
For sentient beings of the final age who practice this, they will escape false views.
If one compares this with the verses, the extent of their expansion or brevity can be known.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I request the majestic demeanor for requesting the Dharma.

O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, I pray that for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas here, and for all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who cultivate the Mahāyāna, you will explain how they should practice upon hearing of this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment. World-Honored One, if those...
Sentient beings who know that all things are like illusions find that their own bodies and minds are likewise illusory. How can they use illusion to further cultivate within illusion?
If the nature of all illusions were entirely extinguished, there would be no mind; who then would perform cultivation? Why, then, do you say that cultivation is like an illusion?
If sentient beings fundamentally do not engage in cultivation, they will forever dwell amidst the transformations of birth and death, never [attaining liberation].
Having understood that all realms are like illusions, how can the mind of discursive thought be liberated?

We pray that you will provide expedient means for all sentient beings of the final age, so that they may practice gradually and successively, enabling all beings to forever leave behind all illusions.

When the Great Being Samantabhadra heard the preceding exposition, he followed its traces and gave rise to doubt; therefore, he specifically requested instruction on the skillful means for cultivation.

Based on what the Buddha had previously taught—that these are like flowers in the sky and thus there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death—he attained sudden enlightenment in a single thought-moment.
Having thus immediately realized the nature of birth and death, he did not require further effort.
To practice cultivation is to have no other expedient means; this is a matter of great disparity, and one who is not of the highest capacity cannot comprehend it.
Alas, among the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age, those of the highest capacity are few. If they do not rely on cultivation, it will be difficult for them to attain awakening and entry.
If they do not rely on expedient means, they will be unable to engage in cultivation. Therefore, he first asks about cultivation.

This seeks the gradual method of skillful means. If one were to say that knowing these are like flowers in the sky means there is no more cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), yet flowers in the sky are themselves illusory and false.

Even if there were sentient beings capable of knowing that body and mind are like illusions, if that which is known is an illusion, then this knowing subject—the body and mind—is itself also an illusion. How then can [an illusion]...
"Is one still practicing illusion? This is the first doubt. If the illusion of the known has already ceased, then the illusion of the knower must also cease.
If both the subject and object thus cease, then there is no mind. Furthermore, who would be the practitioner?
How then can it be said that practice is like an illusion? This is the second doubt. If [these] various...

Sentient beings fundamentally do not rely upon cultivation. If this were so, they would perpetually dwell within the midst of birth and death as mere illusions, never understanding the illusory nature of their own realm; how then could they liberate their deluded minds?
This is the third doubt. For this reason, I inquire of the Tathāgata: I pray that you will explain the skillful means of cultivation, so that all sentient beings may [attain liberation].

This gives rise to the eternal departure from all illusions. Therefore, below, the World-Honored One answers: "By means of the illusory mind of sentient beings, one returns to the extinction of illusion;
it does not hinder using illusion to cultivate illusion. This constitutes one answer. When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving.

"Not entering into annihilation" constitutes the second answer. "Knowing that illusions are such is itself liberation; there is no further expedient means. Being liberated from illusions is itself awakening;
there is no gradual progression. This constitutes the third answer. These collectively explain and fulfill the intent of the preceding chapter regarding sudden awakening and sudden cultivation.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. They made this request three times, beginning again and again from the end.
This describes the earnest sincerity of their quest for the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family, you..."

To enable all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age to cultivate the bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi, I shall explain the expedient means and gradual stages that allow all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
This concludes the praise, the inquiry, the exhortation to listen, and the permission to speak.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, together with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence.
This is to joyfully receive the sound of the Dharma and, with a darkened mind, wait in expectation to hear it.
Good son, the various illusory transformations of all sentient beings are all produced from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*).
They are like flowers in the sky that arise from space; though the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings likewise...
When illusion ceases, all illusions are extinguished; the awakened mind remains unmoving.
This answer shows that the extinction of all illusions does not entail falling into nihilism.

To speak of awakening based on illusion is itself called an illusion. If one speaks of there being awakening, one has still not departed from illusion; yet to speak of there being no awakening—[is likewise so].
It is likewise so. Therefore, the extinction of illusion is called "immovability.
This answer uses illusion to cultivate illusion in order to explain and establish the meaning of not falling into annihilationism. That is to say, one uses awakening to awaken to illusion;
yet awakening itself is also illusion. Thus it is said: "To speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion. If one speaks of illusion...
That which is extinguished yet has awakening remaining is also an illusion. Therefore it is said: "If one says that awakening exists, one has not yet escaped illusion.
If one further gives rise to a view and says that both illusion and awakening are non-existent, this too is an illusion. Why is this so?
This is because one has not yet reached the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One must simply dispense with both existence and non-existence, so that the essence of illumination stands alone.

Thus it is said: "The extinction of illusions is called immovability. Since all manner of illusory transformations arise from the wondrous mind of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfectly awakened enlightenment), when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoved.
Good son, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they firmly maintain this mind of distancing, even that mind which is like an illusion is likewise distanced.
This demonstrates the skillful means for transcending illusion, answering the request to be forever free from all illusions, and thereby dispelling the very mind that seeks to transcend illusion.
It means that only by knowing something is an illusion does one give rise to the mind capable of transcending it.

Once all illusions have ceased, if one stubbornly clings to the existence of a mind capable of transcending them, this mind is itself like an illusion; therefore, it too must be further abandoned. This is the dispensation.
This is the mind capable of detachment at the first level.
To distance oneself from illusion is itself a form of detachment; one must further distance oneself from this [detachment].
This refers to the removal of the detachment belonging to the second level. That is to say, when one first uses knowledge to detach from illusion, the illusion is extinguished. Then...
Send forth the mind that is capable of knowing; if that which knows has been extinguished, then this very detachment is likewise like an illusion. Therefore it is said:
"To distance oneself from [delusion] is itself an illusion, and one must further distance oneself from that [detachment]."
One distances oneself from distancing, and likewise distances oneself from that distancing.
This refers to the removal of the third layer of distancing—the distancing of the aforementioned distancing—which is called "the removal of the removal.
When there is nothing further to be distanced, all illusions are eliminated; it is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood act as cause and condition, fire emerges and the wood is consumed.
Ashes fly and smoke vanishes. To cultivate illusion with illusion is likewise so. When all illusions are extinguished, one does not enter into annihilation.
These words mean that one eliminates again and again until there is nothing more to eliminate; thus it is said: "When there is nothing further to depart from, all illusions are removed.
The metaphor of drilling for fire represents the various illusory wisdoms; the ashes flying and the smoke vanishing represent successive eliminations. There remains only the ground.
Because it exists, it is likened to not entering into annihilation. This summarizes the intent of the answer to the question.
Good son, to know illusion is to be detached from it; no expedient means need be employed. To be detached from illusion is awakening itself; there is no gradual progression.
This conclusion demonstrates sudden awakening and sudden realization, thereby manifesting the principle of the ultimate single mind.

A question is raised: "In the preceding response, you explained that illusory cultivation is illusory and that one must repeatedly negate even those negations; these were all intended as expedient means following a gradual sequence.
Now, in this conclusion, you state that there are no expedient means and no gradual sequence. Is it not the case that the Buddha’s own words are contradictory?"

"Yes. He replied, "This meaning is profound and mysterious; it is truly difficult to realize. It was stated above that all various illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi-citta*).
Although it speaks of repeated negation and sweeping away, that which is negated and swept away is, in its entirety, but a single illusion.
This means that within this wondrously enlightened mind, if there is the slightest arising of thought or movement of consciousness, the state of seeing [the truth] has not yet been attained."
Forget it. All that is pervasive is illusion. If you know that, in the final analysis, everything is illusion, then all illusions will naturally fall away.

It is simply a matter of knowing; why then employ any further expedient means? If you merely maintain a mind of attachment, this indicates that your knowledge and views have not yet been forgotten, which is termed "subtle clinging to dharmas" (*dharmagrāha*).
Once you thoroughly realize that all things are illusory, they will vanish on the spot.
The whole body manifests spontaneously; therefore it is said: "To know illusion is itself to leave it; to leave illusion is itself awakening. This is just like a fragrant elephant crossing a river:
with a single step, it reaches the bottom. As it is said: "There is no need for expedient means, nor is there any gradual progression."
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should practice according to this; only by doing so can they forever leave behind all illusions.
This concludes the response to the question, meaning that it is necessary to repeatedly eliminate and sweep away [delusions] in this manner before one can forever be free from them.
All are illusions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Samantabhadra, you should know: All sentient beings, Since beginningless time, have been subject to illusory ignorance."
All [phenomena] are established from the Perfect Enlightenment Mind of all Tathāgatas.
Just as flowers in the sky appear with forms depending upon space, yet when these illusory flowers vanish, space itself remains fundamentally unmoving;
so too do illusions arise from various states of awakening. When the illusion ceases, awakening is perfected, for the mind of awakening is inherently unmoving.
If those bodhisattvas, as well as sentient beings of the final age, always distance themselves from illusions, all illusions will be entirely left behind.
Just as fire is produced within wood, when the wood is exhausted, the fire naturally extinguishes;
awakening has no gradual stages, and skillful means are likewise so.
The prose merely states that various illusory transformations arise from the awakened mind, yet it does not specify what constitutes these illusory transformations.
Therefore, the verse supplements this with the two characters for "ignorance" (avidyā), meaning that all various illusory transformations are, in fact, ignorance.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I request the majestic demeanor of the Dharma.

O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, we pray that you will expound for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas present here, and for all sentient beings of the future age, the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice:
how one should contemplate and how one should maintain [the teachings], for sentient beings have not yet attained awakening.
By what skillful means can all be universally awakened?
This Universal Eye requests that you explain the gradual practice in order to clarify the meaning of the perfectly illuminating, pure aspect of awakening.
Based on the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter, it was stated directly: "To know that these are but flowers in the sky is to be without cyclic existence, and likewise without a body."
The mind undergoes birth and death therein. The "Chapter on Samantabhadra" states: "To know that it is an illusion is itself liberation;

no expedient means are required. To be liberated from illusion is itself awakening; there is likewise no gradual progression. This refers to the sudden realization of the one mind, attaining immediate and sudden verification without traversing stages and without relying on cultivation;
it requires nothing more than the single character "know. This is something that only those of the highest capacity can achieve.
[One may] realize [this]. However, sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age are such that those of the highest faculties are few, while those of middling and inferior faculties are many.
If they do not practice, they will remain forever in birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If they practice without the correct expedient means (*upāya*), there will be no door through which to enter.

Furthermore, without gradual stages, it is difficult to achieve sudden awakening (*tunwu*). Question: Contemplation (*siwei*) is the initial application of the techniques for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Abiding in the practice is the principle for settling the mind; it is, in every respect, a skillful means for awakening.

World-Honored One, if those sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct reflection, they will become confused and distressed upon hearing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, and will be unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment. I pray that you will arouse compassion and act for my sake.
For those of equal standing and sentient beings in the final age, these are provisional teachings of skillful means.
This repeated request concerns the necessity of skillful means. Regarding "contemplation": one must first rely on correct skillful means to enter the gate;
only then can one attain correct contemplation. Furthermore, because skillful means are considered urgent, he concludes the request for them.
It is so. As for "provisional designation": because one establishes skillful means within that which lacks skillful means, it is merely a provisional designation.
According to the beginning of the subsequent answer, relying on *śamatha* (calm abiding), maintaining the precepts, and sitting in meditation constitute the true skillful means.

Constantly maintaining this thought—that the union of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (insight) is right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*)—and that what is not illusory does not cease, is to dwell permanently in the state where defiled marks are forever extinguished.
"Extinction! The ten directions are pure; this is awakening.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. He made this request three times, beginning again from the end after each repetition.
Having prostrated three times with utmost sincerity, the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
It is well that you are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of practice and contemplation."
The Abbot, employing various skillful means, said: "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Having thus granted his approval and exhorted them to listen, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, together with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence.
The assembly remained silent and waited.
"Good sons, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure, perfect,
and enlightened mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions."

This is the general response to the intent of the question. Although the Universal Eye (Samantabhadra) asked about the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance, the primary intent of his question was specifically to inquire about the skillful means for the initial mind that is free from illusion; therefore, the Buddha answered with the swift essentials of cultivation.
It is simply by taking right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) as the primary means of practice that it is said, "one should maintain right mindfulness.
Now, right mindfulness is non-thought. Therefore, whenever thoughts arise or the mind moves within the essence of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-āśraya*), they are all illusory transformations.
The intent is that when not a single thought arises, all delusions will naturally cease; hence it is said, "to remain far removed from all illusions."
It was previously stated that all various illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment;

therefore, one must depart from discursive thought in order to attain correspondence with it. As the Treatise says: "The realm of departure from discursive thought can only be realized through direct realization.
This serves as the primary expedient means.
First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, settles the assembly, and dwells in quiet seclusion.
This demonstrates the expedient means for departing from discursive thought. In the Sanskrit language, *śamatha* is translated here as "cessation" (*zhi*).

Now, why must the cultivation of practice take cessation as its primary focus? It is because sentient beings have long identified with the mind of deluded thoughts that clings to and pursues external objects.
Thoughts arise and perish without ceasing for even a moment. Now, one wishes to suddenly leave all thoughts behind; how could this be possible?
Therefore, one first cultivates the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) as the initial effort and the expedient means for entering dhyāna.

Regarding what is called "stopping," according to the Tiantai school, there are three types of stopping: stopping by realizing the true nature (*tattva*), stopping by following conditions through skillful means (*upāya-anuvartana*), and stopping by quelling the two [extremes].

This is the cessation of extreme conceptualization (*anta-vikalpa*). With these three types of cessation as the precursor, one may subsequently enter the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way.
The cessation in this present sutra is exclusively the cessation of realizing reality (*tattva-śamatha*).
If one cultivates this cessation, first set aside the body and mind, both internally and externally, all at once. Letting go again and again until there is nothing further to let go of—then...
When all perceptions cease and both internal and external become one emptiness, within this very state of emptiness, one is able to realize union with the true mind.

When delusive thoughts do not arise, mindfulness naturally departs. Therefore, stillness (*śamatha*) is taken as right mindfulness; if right mindfulness manifests before one, [the mind is stabilized].
Then all delusions are suddenly extinguished; hence it is said that one "remains far removed from all illusions. This is the essential point for entering dhyāna, which students should understand.

As for the firm maintenance of the prohibitive precepts, this corresponds precisely to the three gradual stages of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, wherein one first maintains the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*).

It is as bright and clear as ice and frost; therefore, it is called "firmly maintaining. As for those who sit in quietude within a still chamber, this is because when a practitioner was previously amidst a state of movement and distraction, they could not have gathered their mind without such sitting in quietude.
Using this as proof, since one is no longer engaged in activity, one is simply practicing the "stopping that realizes the true essence" (*tǐzhēnzhǐ*).
However, the requirement that one must dwell peacefully among a community of followers does not necessitate a large number of people; one need only take—
Having those of identical views and identical conduct as one’s refuge makes it easy to resolve upon and accomplish practice.

One should constantly reflect: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements—namely, hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and filth—which all return to earth;
and saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, foam, phlegm, tears," and so forth.
The vital essence, as well as excrement and urine, all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement and transformation return to wind.
When the four great elements each depart, where then will this delusory body reside? One thus knows that this body ultimately has no substance;
it exists as a manifestation of combination, truly like a magical illusion. Through the provisional conjunction of the four conditions, the six sense faculties falsely arise.
This demonstrates the method for entering contemplation, answering the question regarding gradual reflection. First, the provisional contemplation (*jia guan*) is shown.
Now, regarding the question on the gradual expedient means of universal vision (*puyan*), it stems from the passage in the Mañjuśrī chapter which states:

"One falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind. It further says, "Know these to be empty."

When flowers are absent, there is no turning of the wheel. It is further said: "To know illusion is itself liberation; no expedient means need be employed. This constitutes sudden awakening and sudden realization.
However, fearing that those of middling or inferior faculties might be unable to enter this suddenly, he makes this request.

The World-Honored One first demonstrated the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) as a preliminary expedient; now he demonstrates the entry into *vipaśyanā* (insight), directly answering the question regarding contemplation. First, he demonstrates...
Regarding the method of contemplating the provisional (conventional): in the initial teaching, one contemplates the body by means of successive analysis, and subsequently contemplates the mind;
this demonstrates the method of gradual progression. Furthermore, there are three modes of contemplation, namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Now, according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, through the "illusory-like samādhi," it is shown that one first enters emptiness from the provisional, and subsequently enters the middle from both emptiness and the provisional; this precisely reveals the practice.
Regarding the gradual progression of the mind: first, one contemplates the body as being like an illusion; thus, this constitutes the contemplation of the provisional (parikalpita).

When the three contemplations are fully perfected within a single moment of mind, the single character "know" (jñāna) in the previous phrase—"knowing that the illusory is itself detachment"—is explained in its entirety.

The six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally; through the accumulation of delusive conditioning energies within them, there appears a semblance of conditioned phenomena, which is falsely named "mind."
This demonstrates the expedient means for contemplating the mind. The six sense organs are internal; the four great elements are external, as are the six sense objects derived from them.
Because the organs and objects combine, consciousness arises within them; hence it is said they "combine to form" [the world].
The phrase "falsely existing below" indicates that the mind is provisional. This means that the mind manifest before us is merely deluded thought (*vikalpa*), not the true mind. How is this known?
Thus, these six consciousnesses grasp at the shadows of the five preceding sense-objects that have fallen away.

Through the accumulation of the energy of these objects, there appear semblances of false forms; these are merely shadows of deluded thought, falsely named "mind. Beings in their daily lives recognize only these false shadows as the mind.
Now, when one observes this mind, it has no essence apart from its objects. If one does not recognize [it as such]...
If the provisional is treated as the real, deluded thoughts will naturally vanish. At the very point where deluded thoughts vanish, one need not seek the Real, for the Real spontaneously returns;
thus, this serves as the expedient means for the contemplation of the provisional.
Good son, this deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense objects. When the four great elements are decomposed, no sense objects can be found;
therein, the conditions for sense objects each return to their dispersal and extinction, such that ultimately no perceiving mind can be seen.

This demonstrates the successful completion of the contemplation of the provisional (conventional truth). As stated previously: "One falsely identifies the reflected images of the six sense objects as the characteristics of one's own mind.

If one merely knows that these are illusions, one cannot immediately transcend them; therefore, the teaching first instructs one to contemplate that this body, composed of the four great elements, is provisional and will eventually disperse and perish.
Once the internal faculties are no longer present, there are likewise no external objects to confront them. Thus, both faculty and object...
Once they have been eliminated, the mind that takes them as objects also ceases; this mind, too, is merely provisional.
Good son, for those sentient beings, because the illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease;
because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of the illusion also ceases. When the cessation of the illusion has ceased, that which is not illusory does not cease. This is, for example, like...
"Just as when polishing a mirror, once the grime is exhausted, its clarity appears.

This demonstrates the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional. It means that through contemplative observation, the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness has all been extinguished.
Since that which is observed is empty, the observer also vanishes; thus it is said, "When the illusion is extinguished, that which extinguishes it is also extinguished. Because of this...
It is said that one who knows empty space perceives it as the appearance of flowers in the sky; therefore, even the act of contemplative observation does not arise.
This constitutes the mutual forgetting of subject and object, wherein all opposition is severed. There remains only the perfectly round, luminous, and pure true mind.

Thus it is said: "That which is not illusory is indestructible; the awakened mind is unmoving. "Purity" is a synonym for "emptiness," hence it is called the "contemplation of emptiness. The analogy of the mirror can serve to illustrate this.

"Know this, son of good family. You should know that both body and mind are entirely illusory defilements. When the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure.

This proceeds from emptiness and the provisional to enter the Middle Way. This refers to the initial statement: "All are based upon the characteristic of the perfectly illuminating, pure state of awakening."
However, because it is the single mind, it is called the Middle Way.
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects five colors, appearing differently according to the direction from which it is viewed.
Foolish people, seeing that maṇi, believe that the five colors truly exist within it. Good son, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment likewise manifests...
Body and mind respond to each according to their respective types. Those who are deluded likewise claim that pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such self-characteristics of body and mind.
Because of this, they cannot distance themselves from illusion and transformation. Therefore, I say that body and mind are illusory defilements.

In contrast to being free from these illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva. When the defilements are exhausted and the contrast is removed, there is neither the defilement to be contrasted nor any further designation.

"Name" (ming) here reveals the absolute, non-dependent true mind, demonstrating the essence of the perfectly illuminating and pure state of awakening. The mani-jewel metaphor represents the perfectly illuminating pure mind;
its manifestation of the five colors represents the five aggregates (skandhas) of body and mind. The old commentary states that it is a metaphor for...
"The five paths" is an overly broad reference. Since the sutra speaks of the "self-characteristics of body and mind," it specifically refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
However, the phrase "according to their types" intends to encompass all beings of the five paths. Nevertheless, the correct meaning specifically points to the sentient beings of the five paths;

they are collectively nothing other than the body and mind of the five aggregates. This is because the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind originally possesses no five aggregates; it is solely due to ignorance and karma that [they appear].
It is produced by illusion, for it manifests entirely from the wondrous mind.

Just as a mani jewel appears in five colors according to conditions, sentient beings fail to understand the true mind and instead recognize only the illusory appearances of the five aggregates. This is like a foolish person who clings to the idea that the substance of the jewel actually possesses five colors.
Because they mistakenly take the five aggregates to be the self, thereby obscuring the true essence, they are called "illusory defilements."
Now, by means of the wisdom of contemplation, one illuminates and shatters through the emptiness of the five aggregates; thus one is called a Bodhisattva.

Yet, because the sense of duality has not been forgotten, this is still ignorance, and the true essence remains unmanifest. If the sense of duality is entirely forgotten, such that both subject and object are simultaneously severed, only then is the absolute, non-referential true mind revealed.

Good son, because these Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all things are illusory and have extinguished their reflected images, they then attain a purity that is directionless.
This is manifested by the awakening to boundless empty space; because this awakening is perfect and luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind.
This precisely reveals the characteristic of perfect illumination. It means that this wondrous, perfect essence of mind is fundamentally numinous, luminous, vast, and profoundly tranquil;
it is called "true emptiness. Initially, due to a single thought of ignorance, this wondrous luminosity was obscured.

Thus, the substance of true emptiness was transformed into the stubborn void of the ten directions. Now that ignorance has been shattered, the vacuities of the ten directions have all utterly dissolved.
Therefore, one contemplates that the vacuity of the ten directions manifests from the awakened mind;
yet, once the vacuity has dissolved, the wondrously luminous essence is revealed. Hence it is said that the mind is manifested as pure. When this mind is once purified—

Thus, there would be no dharma-realm among the ten that is not pure. Therefore, the subsequent passage systematically clarifies that the bodies, minds, and realms of both sages and ordinary beings are each and every one pure;
this is precisely what was previously termed the "characteristic of pure awakening. Now, "purity" is an alternative name for emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
From here until the section on "equanimity and immovability," the text collectively demonstrates the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness.
Because the mind is pure, the objects of sight are pure. Because the objects of sight are pure, the eye faculty is pure.
Because the eye faculty is pure, eye-consciousness is pure. Because consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure. Because the objects of hearing are pure, the ear faculty is pure.
Because the faculties are pure, auditory consciousness is pure. Because consciousness is pure, the perception of objects is pure.
This is likewise so for the nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This reveals the aspect of the perfect illumination of the essence of the wondrously awakened mind, thereby demonstrating the nature of emptiness. This "seeing-dust" specifically refers to the deluded seeing of ignorance;
it is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. It perfectly reflects the six gates of perception.

This seeing is itself the dust, not the dust of form. This means that the mental states and objects of the ten dharma realms—both deluded and awakened—all exist in dependence upon this deluded seeing.
Now, with the single destruction of ignorance, the wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous; subject and object both vanish, and the duality of agent and action is severed.
This very vision also subsides, whereby the ten realms of existence are swept away into pure clarity. Because they are thus purified, each and every one is omnipresent.

The single, wondrous luminosity universally illumines the Dharma-realm; therefore, the subsequent text enumerates the mental states of each of the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones, stating that each is pure and all-pervasive.
According to the underlying principle, this is simply the single mind’s universal illumination, wherein the shadows of both the holy and the ordinary are utterly extinguished.
However, because the teaching is directed toward those who have not yet attained awakening, the subsequent text proceeds to enumerate each case one by one to manifest its perfect clarity.
This is the wondrous nature of universal pervasiveness. Furthermore, first demonstrate the purity of the six mundane realms.
Good son, because the sense faculties are pure, the objects of form are pure; because form is pure, the objects of sound are pure;
and it is likewise for the objects of fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

This correctly refers to the purity of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Since it uses this term for the "six sense objects," we know that the previously mentioned "object of seeing" is not among these six;
rather, it points to deluded seeing itself as being the object.
Good son, because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure;
and the fire and wind elements are likewise so.
This refers to the purity of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Son of good family, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), and the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) are pure.

This statement generally indicates that the mental objects and states of all six classes of ordinary beings are entirely pure. The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are the sense organs and environments of ordinary people;
