the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) constitute the triple world (*tridhātu*), serving as the ground for the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of sentient beings.
In summary, the body, mind, and the world—all are entirely pure. This precisely accords with [the teaching of] the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The meaning of the "purity of the six sense faculties" is identical [in both texts]. That sutra merely speaks of the Dharma-preacher who upholds the sutra;

such a person, being at the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), immediately attains the purity of the six sense faculties. This statement—that awakening is sudden and that only the mind exists—implies that both the ordinary and the sage are simultaneously obliterated.
Throughout the four noble stages that transcend the world, all [faculties] are pure. The "six ordinary beings" mentioned above and the "four noble ones" mentioned below are pure;
therefore, there are the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure; likewise, even up to the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors, all are completely pure.
This enumerates how the four noble supramundane realms are entirely pure.
Good son, because the nature of all true marks is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure;
because many bodies are pure, in this way, even up to the sentient beings of the ten directions, their perfect enlightenment is pure.

This is intended to reveal the perfect purity of the sense-faculties, the physical body, and the world. Herein, first the primary retribution—the single body as well as the manifold bodies—is presented.
There are no sentient beings whatsoever who are not pure; yet, the sentient beings of the ten directions are perfectly awakened and pure.
Thus, sentient beings are suchness.
Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure;
because many worlds are pure, it extends in this way until the very end of empty space, encompassing the three periods of time in their entirety—all are equally pure and immovable.
By contemplating this example, one sees that the dependent world of retribution is pure. Thus, the realm of sentient beings is empty;

the distinction between the holy and the ordinary is equally dissolved, leaving only the single, pure, perfectly luminous, and precious awakening. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "I, by means of non-arising and non-ceasing..."
This accords with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha is neither a worldly dharma nor a supramundane dharma, for all dharmas are the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, each subsequent instance is described as "immovable."
Good son, just as space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.

Because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable. In this way, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors being equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.
Sentient beings in the world of empty space exist because they are deluded regarding the nature of enlightenment.
Now, when all phenomena accord with Perfect Enlightenment, they are equal and equal, quiescent and non-dual; therefore, it is said to be "immovable.

This merely manifests the sublation of all phenomena, which corresponds to the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). By subsuming phenomena back into principle, and since principle is omnipresent, phenomena are likewise omnipresent.
Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Each one is all-pervasive.
Good son, the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, pure, and unmoving; because it is perfectly without limit, you should know that the six sense organs pervade the dharma-realm.
Because the sense organs are all-pervasive, you should know that the six sense objects pervade the dharma-realm. Because the sense objects are all-pervasive..."
One knows that the four great elements pervade the dharma-realm; likewise, even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, they pervade the dharma-realm.

This proceeds through the ten dharma-realms to manifest how phenomena follow along with principle in their pervasiveness; this corresponds to the gate of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena within the dharma-realm.
This demonstrates the meaning of the contemplation of the provisional.
Good son, because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled.

Because the faculties and objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled, it is likewise so even up to the gates of *dhāraṇī*, which are neither destroyed nor intermingled, like hundreds of thousands of lamps.
The light illuminates a single room; this light pervades everywhere, being neither destroyed nor mixed.
This traverses the ten dharma-realms to manifest the contemplation of the all-encompassing containment of the dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).

This corresponds to the meaning of the Middle Way within a single mind. This clarifies that the characteristics of the dharma-realm and the single mind exist within one another without confusion, each remaining undestroyed.
By virtue of these characteristics, the meaning of Perfect Enlightenment’s universal illumination is established.
Good son, because enlightenment is thus accomplished, you should know that the Bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas;
they do not loathe birth-and-death nor crave nirvana; they do not revere those who uphold the precepts nor detest those who violate them; they do not prize long-standing practice nor...
Do not disparage beginners. Why? Because they possess all-encompassing awareness. It is like the light of the eyes clearly perceiving objects before it;
that light is perfect and complete, free from both aversion and attachment. Why? Because the essence of light is non-dual and devoid of aversion and attachment.
This demonstrates that quiescent extinction is the single mind, equal and non-dual; it precisely reveals the characteristic of pure awakening.
For bondage and liberation, hatred and love, and so forth, are all dualistic appearances. These dualistic appearances arise from the deluded vision of ignorance.
Now, through perfect illumination, all things are awakened; therefore, there is no duality. The "eye-light" is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eighth consciousness. Perfect...

It illuminates all the sense faculties; because it is most manifest in the eye, it serves as a metaphor for the essence of universal illumination and non-duality of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
Good son, when these bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age cultivate this mind and achieve accomplishment, there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment therein.
Universal illumination is quiescent extinction and non-dual. Within this, hundreds of thousands of millions...

Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of unspeakably many hundreds of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers arise and perish in confusion like flowers in the sky—neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor liberated.
Only then does one realize that sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning;
birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.
This is a further explanation of the aforementioned characteristics of universal enlightenment, quiescent extinction, and non-duality, in order to manifest the ultimate realization of the one mind.
This is because within the *tathāgatagarbha*, there are fundamentally no characteristics of delusion or awakening, birth and death, or coming and going.
Nevertheless, both birth and death and nirvāṇa are merely matters occurring within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is shattered, [one turns back...]
View past events as nothing more than a dream from yesterday.
Good son, because they are like a dream from yesterday, you should know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa are without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going.
That which is realized is without gain and without loss, without grasping and without abandoning. As for that which is able to realize it, there is no...
Activity is without cessation; there is no undertaking and no extinction. Within this realization, there is neither subject nor object;
ultimately, there is no realization, nor is there one who realizes. The nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible.
This is a further demonstration that the essence of the single mind of ultimate quiescence is fundamentally non-dual.
It was previously stated that from within the nature of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-āśraya) flow forth all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the various *pāramitās*.

This means that when one is deluded regarding pure *tathatā*, it becomes the phenomena of birth and death for sentient beings composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). [The same applies to] *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
The fruits realized are the various *pāramitās*, which serve as the practices that realize them.
Since within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is fundamentally no coming or going, nor delusion or awakening, nor birth and death, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday.

If they are like a dream from yesterday, how could there be any matter of cultivation, realization, gain or loss, or acceptance and rejection? Since there is neither cultivation nor realization, then...
There is neither subject nor object. All images are ultimately quiescent. Such dharmas as these are all truly, eternally abiding and indestructible.

This is the ultimate state of the pure aspect of awakening that perfectly illumines the dharma-realm; thus, it provides a comprehensive explanation for the first chapter, all of which is based on the meaning of the pure aspect of awakening that perfectly illumines.
Good son, those bodhisattvas, practicing in this way, progressing through these stages, contemplating in this manner,
maintaining themselves in this way, employing such skillful means, and attaining awakening in this manner, seek such a Dharma without becoming confused or distressed.
These concluding words of response refer back to the primary practice; therefore, they all state, "Thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Universal Eye, you should know: all sentient beings have bodies and minds that are like illusions.
Their physical forms depend upon the four great elements, and their mental natures revert to the six sense objects.
Since the substances of the four great elements are each distinct, what is it that brings them together? By practicing in this way gradually, everything becomes entirely pure.
Immovable and pervading the Dharma-realm, Without effort, cessation, spontaneity, or extinction, And likewise no one who can realize it— All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky;
The three periods of time are entirely equal, Ultimately without coming or going.
Whether it be Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds Or sentient beings of the final age, [they are all thus].
"Those who wish to enter the Buddha-way should practice in this manner.
The meaning of these verses is as can be understood from the text.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and [circumambulated him] to the right.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, knelt for a long time with palms joined,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One of Great Compassion will, for the sake of all the assembly of Bodhisattvas, skillfully proclaim the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect awakening."
The gradual expedients of the practice of the causal stage of the Great Dhāraṇī opened up the ignorance of all sentient beings.
The assembly of practitioners present there, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, saw their illusory cataracts cleared away and their eyes of wisdom purified.

This is an expression of gratitude. It follows from the previous Buddha’s statement that it is "like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky," which was taught above to show that the faculties, the body, and the world are all fundamentally pure, like the falling shadows of flowers in the sky. Therefore, this thanksgiving says:
"The illusory cataracts have cleared away, and the eye of wisdom is pure."
"Bhagavān, if all sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all manner of ignorance?
If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been enlightened from the beginning?

If ordinary beings throughout the ten directions have been established in the Buddha-way from the beginning and subsequently give rise to ignorance, when will all the Tathāgatas ever again give rise to anything?"
O Afflicted One, we pray that you will not forsake your unimpeded great compassion; for the sake of all bodhisattvas, reveal the treasury of secrets,
and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, enable them to hear such sūtra teachings and definitive dharma-gates, so that they may forever sever doubt and regret.
This Vajragarbha, having heard the Buddha’s single statement that sentient beings are primordially enlightened, suddenly gave rise to three doubts;
therefore, he posed this question. His intention was as follows: the Buddha initially stated that sentient beings [suffer] due to beginningless ignorance.
Because one falsely identifies with the body and mind, there is birth and death. Furthermore, it is said that one must eternally sever ignorance (*avidyā*) before attaining the Buddha-way;
this implies that ignorance is inherently present within sentient beings. How, then, can it also be said that sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas?
If sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, why is there still ignorance?
If sentient beings were originally Buddhas and subsequently gave rise to ignorance, then when would all the Tathāgatas—who are already perfected Buddhas—ever again give rise to all afflictions?
This is because one hears that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the beginning and that ignorance has been eternally severed.
Because these words contradict the statement that he was about to achieve the Way of the Buddha, he harbored three successive doubts and thus posed this question.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
Having prostrated three times with utmost sincerity, at that time the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound secrets and ultimate..."
This is the ultimate skillful means, the supreme instruction for all bodhisattvas, and the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna.
It enables the bodhisattvas practicing in the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings of the final age, to attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Having praised and granted permission for the instruction,
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the teaching and listened in silence.
As the occasion arose, they waited in expectant stillness.

"Good son, in all worlds, from beginning to end, birth and death, before and after, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, arising and ceasing—these continuous successions of moments, revolving back and forth, and all various acts of grasping and rejecting, are entirely saṃsāra.

To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment without having escaped saṃsāra is impossible; that nature of Perfect Enlightenment would then be identical to the cycle of transmigration. There is no way to avoid saṃsāra [in such a manner]."
This intent is to reprimand those who, with minds subject to arising and ceasing, should not falsely debate the essence of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

For the causes and effects of delusion and awakening within the ten dharma realms are all matters pertaining to the realm of birth and death; they exist only through false perception. Within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, these things do not originally exist.
If one were to debate Perfect Enlightenment by means of false perception, then this enlightened nature would likewise become identical [to that which it is not].
This concerns the phenomena of birth and death. There are three kinds of worlds:

namely, the world of the primary retribution of sentient beings, the world of their secondary retribution, and the world of the Buddhas as perfect awakening through wisdom. These collectively encompass the causes and effects of the support and the supported within the ten dharma realms.
"Beginning" refers to the cause of delusion regarding the fundamental nature; "end" refers to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Birth and extinction pertain to sentient beings.

Body and mind encompass the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. "Before and after" refers to the three periods of time—past, future, and present—whereby the past and future encompass the present.

"Existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing" refers to the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of the world; "existence and non-existence" here specifically refers to the periods of abiding and emptiness.
Gathering and dispersing constitute formation and destruction. Arising refers to the birth and death within the triple world; ceasing refers to the nirvana of the two vehicles.
Such matters as these are but false views and deluded thoughts, continuing in succession from moment to moment.

From the beginning, they have been subject to incessant arising and ceasing, revolving in cycles with various acts of grasping and rejecting. All such things are the false views of the cycle of birth and death. If...
To use such false views to discern Perfect Enlightenment is to make the nature of Perfect Enlightenment identical to the phenomena of birth and death;
therefore, it is said that one is "identical to the cycle of transmigration. If one attempts to escape birth and death through false views, there is no such possibility.
This passage generally rebukes such perversity, which is then detailed through metaphors below.
It is like the movement of the eyes causing the still water to appear to shake; or like the whirling of fire seen by a fixed gaze;
it is also like the moon appearing to move when clouds race past, or the shore appearing to shift as a boat travels. It is just so.
These four analogies illustrate false perception. Still water has no waves, yet waves arise because the eyes move;
a fixed eye has no circle, yet a circle appears because of a whirling firebrand; the moon and the shore do not shift, yet they appear to move because of the clouds and the boat.

The still water, the fixed eye, and the moon on the shore collectively serve as metaphors for the enlightened nature (*bodhātman*). The ripples on the water, the whirling firebrand, the drifting clouds, and the moving boat collectively serve as metaphors for deluded perception.
Good son, if the various rotations have not yet ceased, one cannot even find that object to be previously stationary.
This first provides the analogy: the various rotations refer to the ripples on water, the whirling fire-wheel, the drifting clouds, and the moving boat;

"those objects" refers to the still water, the steady eye, the moon, and the shore. This means that if the rotation has not yet ceased, those objects will certainly find it difficult to remain stationary beforehand.

How much more so for those whose minds are defiled by the cycle of birth and death and have never been purified; how could they contemplate the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and not return again to the cycle?
For this reason, you have given rise to the three delusions.
This uses the shallow to illustrate the profound, serving as a general rebuke against delusion and inversion.
The meaning is that even in mundane, superficial matters, if a spinning wheel does not cease, the object upon it cannot remain still;

how much more so when one attempts to discern the pure, wondrous, and eternally abiding nature of awakening through the false views of birth and death—will one not fall into the stream of transmigration? Thus do these three delusions arise.
"This is truly due to the discrimination of false views. This is a general rebuke of the three doubts. Below follows the formal answer to the meaning of the question.

"Good son, it is like a phantom cataract that falsely perceives flowers in the sky. If the phantom cataract is removed, one cannot say that this cataract has been extinguished and will ever arise again at some time.
Why is this? Because the two dharmas—the cataract and the flowers—are not [inherently] characterized as such."
Because it awaits [conditions]. It is also like the extinction of flowers in the sky; one cannot say that empty space will ever again give rise to flowers in the sky.
Why? Because space originally has no flowers, as they are neither arising nor ceasing.
Birth-and-death and nirvana are likewise subject to arising and ceasing, whereas the wondrous, perfect illumination is free from the obscuration of such flowers.
This uses the single analogy of flowers in the sky to answer the questions collectively and resolve the three doubts. The illusion of cataracts represents the deluded vision of ignorance;
the flowers in the sky represent birth-and-death and nirvana; and empty space represents the wondrously enlightened true mind.

This universally reveals that both birth-and-death and nirvana are all but the flower-like appearances of frantic toil and inverted perception, which fundamentally do not exist within the wondrous, perfect mind.

Regarding this matter, Kāṅgàng now has a doubt. Having heard in the opening chapter that the Buddha taught ignorance (*avidyā*) is the deluded recognition by sentient beings of their illusory body and mind as being inherently existent, it follows that sentient beings exist precisely because of ignorance.
If this is so, why does he further say that sentient beings are originally enlightened Buddhas? If sentient beings were originally...
If one were to become a sentient being after having been a Buddha, that would mean ignorance exists within the Buddha’s own mind.
If this were so, how could afflictions ever arise again within the minds of all Buddhas to cause them to become sentient beings?
These three successive doubts all arise from the discrimination of false views; they stem solely from not yet awakening to the wondrous, perfect true mind. Therefore, first...
This collectively assigns the blame to the inverted views of saṃsāra and answers them all at once through the metaphors of cataracts and flowers in the sky.
If one realizes that the sky is fundamentally devoid of flowers, why doubt that sentient beings are originally enlightened?
If one understands that flowers arise from cataracts, why then doubt that afflictions might arise after attaining Buddhahood? This is the Tathāgata’s skillful instruction.
Once this analogy is understood, the three doubts will be instantly resolved.
Good son, you should know that empty space is neither temporarily existent nor temporarily non-existent;
how much more so for the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment, which accords with it as the equal, fundamental nature of space? Good son, it is like refining gold ore: the gold is not...
Once the ore has been smelted into gold, it does not become ore again. Even after an infinite period of time, the nature of the gold remains unimpaired;
one should not say that it was originally not accomplished. The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is also like this.

This specifically demonstrates that the wondrous, perfect, and eternally abiding true mind does not belong to either birth-and-death or nirvana, thereby providing a further explanation to resolve the doubt regarding the Buddha’s arising of afflictions.

The meaning is this: if even empty space does not follow the arising and ceasing of illusory flowers, how much less so the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, which is the very nature of empty space; furthermore, how could it possibly follow birth-and-death or nirvana?

Does it arise and perish? If one awakens to the fact that the nature of enlightenment is equal, eternally abiding, and immovable, then since all Buddhas have realized this, how could they ever again give rise to delusion?
Therefore, the analogy of refining gold is used to conclude and demonstrate this point.

If one understands this analogy, then although sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, their present ignorance does not prevent them from attaining perfection through cultivation; it is just as gold, though inherently present, [must be refined].
Now, within the ore, it is only after smelting that it is finally seen. This means that while the Buddha-nature is inherently present, one must diligently cultivate it;
while delusion is fundamentally non-existent, it must be severed. If one knows that the nature of gold is indestructible, how could one doubt that the Buddha could again give rise to delusion?
This analogy is concise yet its meaning is profound; thus, the doubts of Vajragarbha were dispelled like melting ice without waiting for every single point to be explained. Below...
This is the definitive teaching.
Good son, in the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally neither bodhi nor nirvāṇa;
there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood; there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor the absence of saṃsāra.
This explicitly demonstrates that within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-gotra), there are fundamentally no marks of birth-and-death or nirvāṇa;
it is intended to resolve the doubts of Vajragarbha. If one awakens to this nature, the deluded views of arising and ceasing will naturally cease to exist.

"Good son, even the perfected realm of the śrāvakas—in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished—can ultimately never reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own direct realization.
How much less could one use a mind of discursive thought to fathom the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment?
It would be like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly; it can never catch fire."
With a mind of saṃsāra, one gives rise to views of saṃsāra; thus, one can never reach the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Quiescent Extinction.
Therefore, I say that all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
This demonstrates that the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) is beyond the reach of thought or mind.

Furthermore, even those of the Two Vehicles, whose bodies and minds have already ceased, cannot yet attain the self-realized Nirvana; how much less can ordinary sentient beings, with their minds of birth and death, hope to enter the wondrous, perfect, and non-arising non-extinguishing nature?
It is absolutely impossible. Therefore, it is likened to a firefly attempting to burn Mount Sumeru—it will ultimately fail.
It is not so. As for those of the Two Vehicles whose body, mind, and speech are all extinguished:

this is because they have severed the discriminating mind of the six consciousnesses, and since the seventh consciousness has been suppressed and does not function, there is no *vitarka* (applied thought) or *vicāra* (sustained thought), nor is there speech.

However, that which they realize as *nirvāṇa* is actually the eighth consciousness in its entirety, wherein ignorance (*avidyā*) is mistaken for *nirvāṇa*. This is because these practitioners of the Two Vehicles lack the name "ignorance."
Because they do not know this, they are unable to personally realize the nirvāṇa that manifests before them. The meaning is this:

if the mental activities of the followers of the Two Vehicles have already ceased, yet they still cannot know the realm of self-realized ignorance, how much less can they—by means of a mind subject to arising and ceasing—seek to enter the Tathāgata’s wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind?
This is certainly impossible; therefore, he uses the metaphor of a firefly to conclude.
This indicates that one should sever the root of saṃsāra; it specifically points to ignorance and deluded vision.

Good son, any conceptualization involving effort arises from the mind; all such things are merely the vaporous conditions of deluded thoughts regarding the six sense-objects, not the true essence of the mind, being like flowers in the sky.
To employ such conceptualization to discern the realm of the Buddha is like using flowers in the sky [to discern something else]. Furthermore...
To bind the fruit of emptiness through successive deluded thoughts—such a thing is impossible.

Good son, this empty and floating mind, with its many clever views, cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). To make such distinctions is not a correct inquiry.
This directly reveals the source of delusion and serves as a reprimand for the one who is the proper recipient of the teaching. The intent is this:

whenever ordinary beings give rise to thoughts or stir their minds, it is all deluded conceptualization and not the true mind. To use such deluded conceptualization to discern the realm of the Buddha is to distance oneself from it by the farthest possible degree.
It is like inviting flowers in the sky and then further producing fruit from that empty space; thus, through successive stages, one only increases one's delusion.
"It is like imagining an ear. How could such a false and floating mind ever accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment?
Therefore, this is not a correct question.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Vajragarbha, you should know that the nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence has never had beginning or end.
If one contemplates it with a mind of saṃsāra, one merely revolves back again;
reaching only the limits of saṃsāra, one cannot enter the ocean of the Buddhas. It is like smelting gold ore: the gold does not exist because of the smelting.
Although gold is originally present within ore, it is only through smelting that its perfection is realized. Once it has become the substance of pure gold, it will never again become ore.
Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are equally like the appearance of flowers in the sky.
Even the act of contemplation is like an illusion; how much more so is the pursuit of what is utterly false?
"If one can thoroughly understand this mind, one may thereafter seek Perfect Enlightenment.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, from among the great assembly, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Regarding the majestic deportment for requesting the Dharma:
the World-Honored One of Great Compassion has extensively opened the secret treasury for the sake of Bodhisattvas, enabling the great assembly to profoundly awaken to saṃsāra,
distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way toward Mahāparinirvāṇa.
They give rise to resolute faith. No longer will they follow the realms of saṃsāra to give rise to views of cyclic existence.
[The text] expresses praise and gratitude. Below, the formal request is set forth:
"World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Nirvāṇa, how..."
When shall we sever the root of saṃsāra? Within all forms of saṃsāra, how many natures are there? In cultivating the Bodhi of the Buddha, what are the various distinctions?
When returning to the midst of worldly toil, how many kinds of skillful means of instruction should be employed to deliver all sentient beings?
We pray that you will not abandon your great compassion for the world, and [instruct] all practicing bodhisattvas as well as sentient beings of the final age.
With the eye of wisdom cleared and purified, one illuminates the mirror of the mind and attains the perfect realization of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.
This formal presentation of the meaning of the inquiry consists of four parts.

Since the Buddha has previously taught that a bodhisattva’s practice begins with severing the root of saṃsāra, the initial question—“How should it be severed?”—intends to ask: what is this root of saṃsāra?
This is the fundamental point. Therefore, the Buddha answers below that craving for affection is the root of saṃsāra.
Second, [the questioner] asks how many natures there are in saṃsāra; the Buddha answers that, due to two kinds of obstacles, there are five distinct natures.
Third, [the questioner] asks how many natures there are in cultivation; the Buddha answers by using those very five natures to manifest the distinctions. Fourth, [the questioner] asks about bodhi—
"How many skillful means does the Bodhisattva employ for the sake of saving sentient beings? The Buddha replied, "Only through great compassion, acting in concert with others, and the power of vows.

However, the question was specifically directed toward those who practice for the sake of both cultivating their own path and benefiting sentient beings. This is because a Bodhisattva’s cultivation is fundamentally undertaken for the purpose of delivering sentient beings;
they do not abandon the realm of sentient beings, for to deliver sentient beings is itself the cultivation of the path.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
The one present for the occasion remained silent and waited.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you..."

"You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous meaning for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, so as to cause the bodhisattvas to purify their eyes of wisdom, and to cause all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, realize the true reality with their minds, and attain the patience of non-arising. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
He praised and approved.
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence,
waiting expectantly.
"Good son, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, have undergone saṃsāra because of various forms of affectionate attachment and craving.
Whether in any world, among any species—be they born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—all take birth and sustain their lives through sexual desire.
You should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root."
This is a direct answer regarding the root of saṃsāra. There are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*): first, the ignorance that initiates karma; second, the ignorance that moistens rebirth.
As for that which initiates karma, it is the very first moment of deluded movement since beginningless time.

Because one is deluded regarding the originally perfect luminosity, it is called ignorance. This, however, is merely being deluded regarding the inherently existing *dharmakāya*, and falsely identifying with the illusory five aggregates.
Regarding "delusively taking the body and mind as the self," this refers to what was explained in the preceding chapter on Mañjuśrī: the fundamental ignorance that has arisen from beginningless time.
Although this involves mistaking the true for the delusive, it has not yet resulted in the continuous succession of birth and death; it merely serves to initiate karma.
Second is the ignorance that moistens birth, which is precisely the root cause of the retribution of the continuous cycle of saṃsāra. This is because...
The ignorance that previously deluded regarding principle falsely identifies the five aggregates—the body and mind—as the self.
Upon this illusory body, one further gives rise to views of male and female, beauty and ugliness, and aversion and attachment, as well as thoughts of craving for sexual desire.
These arise from such love and views, as in the saying: "You love my heart; I cherish your form. Through these causes and conditions, hundreds of thousands of...
For kalpas, they have long remained bound in fetters. Thus, sentient beings are deluded regarding the true nature of the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom;

they take nothing other than the single matter of sexual desire as the very basis for their rebirth and the destiny of their lives. Therefore it is said: "All are caused by sexual desire to determine their nature and destiny.
One should know that within saṃsāra, craving is the root. Consequently, those who now practice cultivation must seek to transcend birth and death.
One may escape the cycle of saṃsāra; therefore, the severance of lust should be regarded as the primary principle. This precisely accords with what is taught in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
whether one is born into the mundane or supramundane realms, or whether there is birth or non-birth, all depends entirely on whether the mind of lust is severed or not.
Thus, this present sutra specifically points to the prior severance of lustful desire as the essential requirement for cultivation.
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
This correctly demonstrates that craving and desire are the root of birth and death.

Since the five aggregates of body and mind of sentient beings originally exist because of craving and desire, and because craving and desire alone constitute the very essence of their life, [they cling to] the objects of greedy desire.
Although they are many, these various desires are all fundamental factors that assist in the arousal of the nature of craving.

Furthermore, it is not only alcohol, meat, and the five pungent herbs that act as auxiliary causes; because the root of craving is already deep, those things that assist in arousing the nature of craving become increasingly thick.
Thus, mind after mind clings to desire, and thought after thought nourishes rebirth. For this reason, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death. Below...
This reveals the root of saṃsāra:

desire arises from craving, and life exists because of desire. Sentient beings cherish their lives, yet they remain dependent upon the foundation of desire; thus, craving and desire serve as the cause.
"Attachment is the fruit.
This clarifies that craving is the root of birth and death. Regarding "desire arises because of attachment":
as stated above, "because various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of attachment," this implies that various desires also arise from attachment. By means of attachment...
It serves as the fundamental basis, for desire acts as its auxiliary cause. Now, "desire" (*chanda*) refers to greed; "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to the root of lust.
That which sentient beings love with a lustful mind is the beautiful form of men and women. Because they crave these forms, they greedily pursue various things:
they provide rich flavors in food and drink to nourish them, use lead-based cosmetics and brocades to adorn them, and supply soft, warm mats and bedding.
They satisfy them with this; even up to using sounds and forms to please them. All desires arise from the mind of lust.

Therefore it is said: "Desire arises because of craving. As for the statement that "life exists because of desire," it is because throughout a sentient being's lifetime, what they are stained by in their desires is the physical form of men and women.
Even after death, when they have relinquished their life and have not yet received their subsequent retribution, [they still...]

There exists an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). This body perceives nothing else; because it seeks the realm of desire, it sees from across thousands of miles the place where men and women are engaged in sexual union.
If there has previously been a karmic affinity of latent passion, it immediately hastens before them and, with the thought that they are male and female, takes them as its own.
When the craving of the heart reaches its peak, it flows along the stream of the saliva of love.
Entering the mother’s womb, one maintains this semen and blood, holding the mental image without relinquishing it; thus, it coalesces into an embryo.
Because this is the source of receiving life, it is said that "life has desire as its cause.

Therefore, that which sustains birth takes craving and desire as its cause, while the subsequent body received as retribution takes the craving for life as its fruit. This is how birth and death continue in succession.
Yet they do not cease. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the characteristics of the continuity of sentient beings are elucidated to clarify this meaning. Below, the state of saṃsāra is shown:

due to objects of desire, various conditions of opposition and compliance arise; when objects run counter to the heart’s attachment, one gives rise to hatred and jealousy, thereby creating all manner of karma.
For this reason, they are reborn again in the realms of hell and hungry ghosts.
This clarifies that the bitter fruits of retribution in the three miserable paths all arise from lustful desire.

Because the fire of craving blazes intensely, one rushes toward the objects of desire; yet these objects may be either adverse or favorable, and if the object accords with one's mind, then craving increases all the more.
If external conditions greatly conflict with one's mind, one will immediately give rise to hatred and jealousy; this may even lead to anger, beating, and verbal abuse, and ultimately to killing.
Thus, there is no evil that one will not commit. Consequently, one invites the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms and the hells;
all of these are brought about by attachment.
Abandoning evil and delighting in good, one again manifests as a human or a deva.

This clarifies that the fruits of the human and celestial realms are induced by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). As stated above, the various karmas created do not, in total, exceed the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*):
namely, the three of the body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and the four of speech—false speech, frivolous speech, malicious speech, and [harsh speech].
Harsh speech and the three mental afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion—these ten unwholesome karmas all arise from craving and desire.
If one commits them fully, one will experience retribution in the three miserable realms; if one neither commits nor avoids them, one will experience rebirth in the human realm;

and if one increases the cultivation of wholesome qualities, one will experience rebirth in the heavens. Thus, humans and devas follow the paths of karma through attraction and aversion, and these too arise from craving.

Furthermore, because one knows that all forms of craving are to be loathed, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Yet, this merely nourishes the root of craving, resulting in the manifestation of superior conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛta-phala*) which are all part of saṃsāra;
thus, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is not realized.

The previous mention of humans and devas refers specifically to the retribution of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is said that these six heavens have not yet severed desire entirely;
they merely refrain from committing evil and are thus moved by the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).

This clarifies that in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and above, sensual attachment does not arise, and they diligently cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). However, as for what they cultivate, they only recognize that sensual desire is defilement, coarse, and an obstacle. Therefore—

Because they feel deep revulsion and detachment, it is said that they "discard craving and delight in relinquishment. Furthermore, because they take joy in the fact that the higher realms are pure, sublime, and free from suffering, they rejoice in and seek to realize them.
Yet, such rejoicing is itself a form of craving; thus, it is said that this merely nourishes the root of craving once again.

For this reason, these are designated only as the superior wholesome fruits of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and do not transcend birth and death. Therefore, it is said that "all of these are within saṃsāra and do not constitute the state of a sage."
The Way truly consists in abandoning attachment by means of attachment; thus, birth and death are not severed.

This is what is meant by saying that even if you cultivate your practice until you reach the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, you still fall short of the second tally of the Chan school, because the emotional roots of birth and death have not been severed.
Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and be freed from the cycle of saṃsāra, they must first sever greedy desire and eliminate craving and thirst.
This summarizes that the root of saṃsāra is entirely the fault of greedy desire and craving thirst.
Good son, when Bodhisattvas manifest transformations within the world, it is not rooted in craving; rather, they do so out of compassion to cause others to relinquish their craving.
They provisionally employ various forms of desire to enter the cycle of birth and death.

If all sentient beings in the final age can renounce all desires and eliminate both hatred and attachment, thereby forever severing the cycle of saṃsāra, and diligently seek the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment—then, regarding...
With a pure mind, one immediately attains awakening.
This explains away doubts and reveals the provisional [teaching]. Fearing that there might be doubt, saying:

"When a Bodhisattva enters the various realms of birth and death, is this not the fault of desire?"—therefore, this explanation says: The Bodhisattva merely manifests desire in order to enter birth and death. Thus...
The inclusion through common purpose involves causing others to abandon greed; this is a provisional manifestation and not a literal reality.
Nevertheless, practitioners must necessarily sever greedy desire; only then can they attain awakening within the pure mind. The above answers the root of saṃsāra;
the following answers the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Good son, all sentient beings, due to fundamental craving and desire, give rise to ignorance, which manifests as five natures that differ and are not equal.

Depending on two kinds of obstructions, they appear with varying degrees of depth and shallowness. What are these two obstructions? The first is the obstruction of principle, which hinders correct knowledge and vision.
The second is the obstruction of phenomena, which perpetuates the cycle of birth and death.

The following answers the question regarding how many types of natures exist within saṃsāra. It states that the two obstacles—those of principle (*li-zhang*) and those of phenomena (*shi-zhang*)—constitute the nature of saṃsāra;

this refers to its essential substance (*ti*). The obstacle of principle is the ignorance that initiates karma (*fa-ye wu-ming*), while the obstacle of phenomena is the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*run-sheng wu-ming*), whereby one revolves through birth and death.
Taking these two obstacles as its substance, there are also distinctions in spiritual practice, which likewise depend on the density of ignorance.
It is manifested through the thinning of the two obstacles to varying degrees of depth.
What are the five natures? Good son, if these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is said not to have attained Buddhahood.

The following is the formal response concerning how many types of natures there are for spiritual cultivation; it first poses the inquiry and subsequently provides the explanation. Regarding the five natures: first, the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-gotra*);
second, the nature of the two vehicles (*dviyāna-gotra*); third, the nature of bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva-gotra*); and fourth, the indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*).
The fifth is the lineage of the five external paths; this is the initial stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

If there are sentient beings who have forever abandoned sensual desire and have first eliminated the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), yet have not severed the obstacles of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), they are only able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, but are unable to manifest and abide in the realm of the Bodhisattva.

This refers to the lineage of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Because those of the two vehicles sever only the three poisons of the six consciousnesses and depart from the death-and-rebirth of the segmented existence (paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa), it is said that they "permanently abandon greed and desire.
As the Sūtra says: "They consider the mere exhaustion of birth-and-death to be nirvāṇa (parinirvāṇa)," yet in reality, they have not attained universal nirvāṇa.
"Good son, if all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should first make a vow to diligently sever the two obstacles.
Once these two obstacles have been suppressed, they will be able to awaken to and enter the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
If the obstacles of phenomena and principle have been eternally severed and extinguished, they will then enter the subtle and wondrous perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata and fulfill Bodhi."

The Great Nirvāṇa. This is the lineage (*gotra*) of these Bodhisattvas. Those of the Three Degrees of Worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) suppress the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa*); those on the Grounds (*bhūmi*) sever the two obstacles. The Treatise says:

"The conceptualized (*vikalpita*) portion of the two obstacles is absent from the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā*); that which is associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses is eliminated stage by stage. After the Path of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-mārga*), [it is otherwise]."
Once it is matured and empty, the two obstacles are forever severed, and one immediately enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvāṇa.
Good son, all sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment; when they encounter a spiritual friend, they follow the practices for the causal stage as performed by that friend.
At that time, their cultivation may be either sudden or gradual. If they encounter the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata...
On the path of cultivation, regardless of whether their faculties are great or small, all attain the fruit of Buddhahood;

this refers to those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*). If one says that all sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), then each and every one of them possesses the lineage of a Tathāgata (*tathāgata-gotra*). How, then, could there be the distinction of being indeterminate? It is simply because of each individual...
Upon encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are instructed according to the Dharma-practices for the stage of cultivation (*bhūmi*) appropriate to each individual.
Through this practice, there arise differences between the sudden and the gradual; this lack of fixed nature depends not on the student's faculties but on the teacher.
This is what is meant by "the seeds being formed through hearing" (*śrutavāsanā*). If one encounters a great spiritual friend, they are guided by means of the Tathāgata’s path of correct cultivation.

Through cultivation, regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This demonstrates that the Buddha-nature is the single cause, while the teachers are not fixed.
Thus, one must personally rely on the most excellent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). In this way, the three vehicles are all subsumed within the indeterminate.
If sentient beings, though seeking virtuous friends, encounter those with false views and fail to attain correct awakening, this is termed the lineage of external paths (tīrthika-gotra).
This is the fault of the misguided teacher and not the fault of the sentient being. These are called the five distinctions of lineage among sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are those of the lineage of heterodox paths. Since it is said that all sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment and none fail to become Buddhas, how could there be anything "heterodox"?
It is simply because they encounter heterodox teachers and heterodox teachings that they become heterodox.

This is merely the fault of the false teacher; it is not the fault of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. This sutra is the Perfect Teaching of the Mahāyāna; there is no capacity that it does not encompass.
It is only because one follows a false teacher that one becomes false. If one abandons the false and returns to the correct, there is not a single person who will not attain Buddhahood.
Herein is seen the principle of the icchantika attaining Buddhahood. The above was the answer regarding the distinctions in cultivation; below—
Answer: This refers to the distinctions of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
Good son, Bodhisattvas enter all worlds solely through the skillful means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇopāya*) to awaken those who have not yet realized the truth.

They even manifest various forms and appearances, as well as circumstances both favorable and adverse, to engage in the same activities as others, transforming them so that they may attain Buddhahood. All [of this is for this purpose].

This answers the question regarding how many skillful means there are for a Bodhisattva to return to the midst of worldly afflictions based on the power of beginningless pure vows. That is to say, although the skillful means by which a Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings are numerous,
they have great compassion as their primary guide, sustained by great vows, and employ the method of "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to gather them in.
This constitutes sublime conduct (*sucarita*). Now, when a Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, they do so through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*):

namely, giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavādita*), beneficial action (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*). Since this sutra emphasizes the severance of desire as its primary concern, it specifically extols cooperation as the sublime conduct for severing attachment.
Were one not sustained by the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and to engage in cooperation recklessly, there would be no avoiding falling [into error].
Therefore, it is essential to rely upon the power of pure vows from time immemorial.
If all sentient beings of the final age should give rise to a superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should make the pure, great vows of a Bodhisattva, speaking these words:
"May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and seek out spiritual friends."
May they not encounter non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles. Relying on their vows, they practice and gradually sever all hindrances.
When the hindrances are exhausted and the vows fulfilled, they shall ascend the pure Dharma-palace of liberation and realize the wondrously adorned realm of Great Perfect Enlightenment.

This statement implies that not only do Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings by relying on the power of their great vows, but even practitioners of the末法 (mofa / degenerate age) must likewise sustain their minds with great vows so as not to fall into false views.

That is to say, when a Bodhisattva practices and gives rise to the *adhimukti-citta* (resolute mind) toward Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vimala-bodhi*), this is one who has resolved to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, first...
He made this vow: "I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and aspire to attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, regarding the spiritual friends I seek, may I not encounter non-Buddhist teachers, heterodox masters, or those of the Two Vehicles with inferior understanding who would destroy my roots of goodness.

May I instead obtain the most supreme spiritual friends who are Bodhisattvas; relying upon their teachings, may I practice and gradually sever all hindrances. If these hindrances are exhausted and my vows fulfilled, then I shall achieve [Buddhahood]."
Thus one attains the fruit of Buddhahood. The realm of wondrous adornment is the ocean of the Buddha’s fruition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Maitreya, you should know that all sentient beings fail to attain great liberation solely because of their craving;

thus they fall into the cycle of birth and death. If they can sever excessive attachment, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion—not through any partiality—they shall all attain the path to Buddhahood.
The prose states: "The five natures differ due to the two obstacles. The verse says:
"If one can suddenly sever the afflictions without being constrained by the distinctions of the five natures, then one shall immediately and suddenly attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
The two obstacles are forever extinguished; Seeking a teacher, one attains right enlightenment.
In accordance with the vows of the Bodhisattvas, one takes refuge in Great Nirvana.

All the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, Through their vows of great compassion, manifest entry into the cycle of birth and death. For those practicing now, And for sentient beings of the final age—

In gratitude for this praise,
I pray that you will once again proclaim for all the assembled multitude of the Dharma the perfect enlightened nature of the Dharma King—
exactly as it was realized and attained by all sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and the World-Honored Tathāgatas— and explain how these differ, so that the multitudes of the final age may [attain it].
Having heard this sacred teaching, one follows it to achieve awakening and can gradually enter [the path].
This inquiry concerns the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment, which is equal for both the holy and the ordinary; why, then, are there distinctions in cultivation and realization?
As previously stated, "Knowing these to be empty flowers, there is no cyclic existence; this is to transcend directly and suddenly attain the stage of Buddhahood, without traversing gradual stages.
Furthermore, it says, "All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment; this is the nature that is fundamentally without differentiation.
To the preceding question regarding differentiation, the Buddha replied that it exists due to the varying degrees of depth of the two obstacles.

Now I ask about the distinctions between cultivation and realization. My intention is this: since the nature of awakening is already equal, the two obstacles likewise cannot constitute any distinction.
I now ask: from the stage of an ordinary person to that of a sage, how can there be distinctions in cultivation and realization?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
The one present for the occasion remained silent and waited.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you..."
"You are indeed able, for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the distinctions of the gradual stages. Listen attentively now;
I shall explain them for you.
He thus granted his approval.
