They waited attentively.
"Good son, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a nature that exists as a nature; it arises in accordance with all natures, yet is without grasping and without realization."
Within the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there are in reality no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings. Why is this? Because both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations.
Since illusory transformations perish, there is no one who attains realization. It is like the faculty of the eye, which cannot see itself;
their nature is inherently equal, yet there is no one who is equal.

Because it was asked how the natures of awakening are one and yet there are differences in the distinctions between the cultivation and realization of sages and ordinary beings, the Buddha first showed that the nature of awakening is fundamentally equal and non-dual. For both Bodhisattvas and sentient beings, there is no sequence of attainment or realization.
Because self-nature is without nature, it is called "non-nature"; because it is possessed by both ordinary beings and sages, it is called "the existence of nature. It follows conditions...
Because it manifests [in this way], it is said to "arise in accordance with all natures. Fundamentally, there is no sequence of cultivation or realization;

rather, it subsequently demonstrates that within the realm of deluded effort, distinctions are revealed. That the eye does not see the eye serves as a metaphor for how the nature of awakening is fundamentally devoid of the duality of subject and object.

Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; unable to eliminate all illusory transformations, they manifest distinctions within the midst of false effort—amidst that which is extinguished and that which is not yet extinguished.
If one attains accord with the Tathāgata’s quiescent extinction, there is in reality neither extinction nor one who extinguishes.

This demonstrates that while sentient beings, due to delusion and inversion, falsely perceive distinctions, in reality there is absolutely nothing to be grasped as subject or object, nor anything to be realized.
Below, the non-differentiation of differentiation is shown. The ancient commentary explains this by means of the Tiantai doctrine of the six identities (*liu ji*).

This means that the nature is inherently equal; because ordinary beings and sages are non-dual, it is called "the principle-as-such" (*li-ji*). As stated above, the enlightened nature is equal, and the principle is fundamentally of one flavor.
Now, because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, and their illusory transformations have not yet ceased, distinctions manifest within the midst of false effort.
This demonstrates that the distinctions of the six stages of "being-as-such" (*ji*) exist due to delusion. If one exhaustively investigates to the ultimate...
The source is quiescent extinction, non-dual. If one thoroughly clarifies the six stages of "being" (*ji*), one will not give rise to arrogance;

if one awakens to the single character "immediacy" (*ji*), one will not give rise to despondency. This is the perfect principle of Tiantai. The above provides a general demonstration of the perfect principle, while the following demonstrates the six stages of "being.
Since this accords with the meaning of the sutra, it is explained accordingly.
Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, due to their deluded conceptions of "self" and "attachment to self," have never known that [the mind] arises and perishes in every thought-moment;
thus they give rise to hatred and love, becoming addicted to the five desires.

This demonstrates the stage of "identity with principle" (*li-ji*). Because sentient beings are entirely immersed in delusion, and because their Buddha-nature exists within that state of delusion, it is called "principle.

Since sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, it is termed "identity with principle. Because they take the awakened nature to be delusive thought, turning their backs on the *dharmakāya* and identifying with the five aggregates, it is said:
"Due to delusive thought, one takes the self; clinging to the delusive body as the self, the view of self becomes firm."

Because they do not abandon their [deluded] nature, it is said that those who love themselves are entirely unaware, moment by moment, that their thoughts arise and perish as they commit various evil karmas.
Yet, the one who commits these acts is precisely the Buddha-nature; therefore, this is called "identity in principle" (li-ji).

If one encounters a virtuous friend who instructs and awakens them to the nature of pure, perfect *bodhi*, causing them to discern its arising and ceasing, they will immediately realize that the nature of this life is inherently characterized by toil and anxiety;
this refers to the stage of "names and words. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding themselves, they do not know their own originally possessed Buddha-nature. If they encounter a virtuous...
Knowledge guides and leads one to realize one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Birth is itself non-birth;

knowing that the fundamental source is Buddha, one understands that the very name and the act of recognizing characters—that single character "knowing" (*jñāna*)—is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Therefore, it is called "the stage of name and character" (*mingzi-ji*).

Furthermore, if there is someone who has forever severed weariness and anxiety and attained the purity of the dharma-realm, yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle for themselves, they will lack mastery over perfect enlightenment.
This is called an ordinary person following along with the nature of enlightenment.

This refers to the stage of practice through contemplation (*guanxing*). This person at the stage of the five grades of practice within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of Tiantai has perfectly suppressed the five abodes of delusion.

Because they have first severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), it is said that "wearisome deliberations are forever severed. Because the three poisons do not manifest, it is said that "the purity of the Dharma-realm is attained.
Because they become attached to this pure state, it is said that "pure understanding becomes an obstruction. Since ignorance remains entirely intact, regarding the Perfect [Teaching]...

Although they have awakened, they lack mastery. Tiantai judges that the stage of practice for the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) and the stage of faith (*xin*) in the Distinct Teaching (*bie*) both sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*jian-si*), and thus they are termed "outer ordinary beings" (*wai-fan*);
therefore, they are collectively designated as "ordinary beings" (*fanfu*).
Good son, for all bodhisattvas, views constitute an obstruction. Although they have severed the obstruction of views, they still abide in the awakening to views;

thus, the obstruction of that awakening constitutes an obstruction for them, and they lack mastery. This is called the state of a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi), wherein they accord with the nature of awakening.
This is the same as the previous case. For those at the stage of the Three Kṣāntis (Three Degrees of Worthiness), their contemplative wisdom has increased in clarity;

they have already perceived that their prior pure understanding was an obstruction, and have now severed it. Although that which was severed has vanished, the contemplative wisdom that performed the severing is termed "seeing-awakening" (*jñāna-darśana*).

This seeing-awakening that performs the seeing becomes an obstruction itself. Because both the subject (the seer) and the object (that which is seen) have not yet been eliminated, one is not yet sovereign within Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Thus it is concluded.
Those called "not yet having entered the stages" specifically refer to the three levels of the virtuous ones (*śaikṣa*).
Good son, both illumination and awareness are equally termed obstructions. Therefore, the Bodhisattva dwells in constant awareness without abiding;
illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescent extinction.

This stage is the "True Suchness with Parts" (*sābhāsa-tathatā*). "Illumination" refers to the object of illumination, which is pure understanding and awakening; "the capacity to observe" refers to the wisdom that perceives, which is seeing and awakening.
These correspond to the two preceding stages, which are both termed "obstructions" because the duality of subject and object has not yet been extinguished.
Now, the Bodhisattvas on the Grounds have already realized the equality of True Suchness; by means of wisdom that is identical to its very essence, they illuminate back toward quiescent extinction.
This is its essence. Therefore, it illuminates yet does not illuminate; because it does not abide in the function of illumination, it is said that "constant awareness does not abide.
Because principle and wisdom are identical as one, they are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished.
It is like a person who cuts off their own head; once the head is severed, there is no one left to cut.
Thus, by using an obstructing mind to extinguish all obstructions, when the obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no one left to extinguish the obstructions.

This uses a metaphor to clarify that both contemplation and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished, such that subject and object are both forgotten. "The person" is a metaphor for the subject that illuminates; "the head" is a metaphor for the object that is illuminated.
Since the object of illumination has vanished, the subject that illuminates is also extinguished; therefore, it is said there is no one who can sever.

However, regarding those who take illumination itself as an obstruction, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "From the arising of the perfect luminosity of illumination. Thus, within the essence of perfect luminosity, there is fundamentally no subject.
However, when one gives rise to a single mind of illumination, it takes form as its object; thus, illumination itself becomes an obstruction.
Since all ignorance is collectively termed "obstruction," and because it is not through illumination that it is extinguished, it is by means of obstruction that obstruction is extinguished.
If all obstructions have already been severed, then even illumination no longer stands; therefore, there is no one who extinguishes obstruction.
The teaching of the sūtras is like a finger pointing at the moon. Once one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
All the various verbal teachings of the Tathāgatas for the sake of instructing bodhisattvas are likewise so.
This reveals the actual realization of Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).

It means that because Bodhisattvas practicing the path have not yet awakened to their own nature (*svabhāva*), the Buddha provisionally employs various verbal teachings to reveal it as a means for awakening the mind. It is like using a finger to point at the moon.

Now that one has realized the nature of one’s own mind, all verbal expressions are merely superfluous teachings. Thus, it is like seeing the moon and knowing that the pointing finger is not the moon itself.
For any discourse concerning cultivation and abandonment, or the subject and object of contemplative wisdom, is but a finger pointing at the moon.
Now that one has realized the single mind, both subject and object are forgotten together, and both contemplation and its illumination vanish simultaneously.
It is quiescent.
This is called the Bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.
This concludes the section on the stages. Because this sutra takes the characteristic of perfect illumination and awakening as its sole principle, the sequence of stages is not discussed.
What is abandoned here concerns only the relative heights of the stages as clarified by the depth of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
If one refers to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra," which states: "One should distance oneself from all illusory and false realms;

because of firmly maintaining this mind of distancing, even when pure understanding has not yet been forgotten, one remains in the stage of contemplative practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). As for the phrase "the mind is like an illusion," it likewise implies distancing.
"Detachment. This means that seeing and awakening are taken as obstacles. At the stage of semblance (sādharmya), there is both awakening and illumination, yet they simultaneously enter quiescence;
thus, one detaches from detachment, which is itself illusory, and further detaches from that detachment. At the stage of partial truth (tathyāṃśa), it is said: "All obstacles are ultimate awakening.
This means one detaches from detachment, and further detaches from the detachment from illusion. When one attains that which has nothing further to detach from, it is called the ultimate.
Awakening. When one reaches ultimate identity, the purport of the sutra becomes clear;
I hope you will contemplate this deeply. Good son, all obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening. Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation.
Whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvana. Wisdom and folly are both universally identified as prajñā. As for bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists...
The Method of Accomplishment: Enlightenment is one and the same; ignorance and suchness are not distinct realms.

All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and folly, are collectively the Brahma-conduct. Sentient beings and their lands share the same dharma-nature; the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands.
Those with nature and those without nature equally achieve the Buddha-way; all afflictions are ultimately liberated. Dharma...
Kṣitigarbha, the ocean of realms illuminates all marks as being like empty space; this is called the Tathāgata’s awakening in accordance with the nature of enlightenment.
This ultimate identity is demonstrated to show the equality of the Buddha-wisdom.

Whether it be the attainment of mindfulness or the loss of mindfulness—these ten pairs of opposing phenomena are all matters pertaining to the extremes of delusion and awakening. This is because the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment does not belong to the duality of delusion and awakening.
Because of cause and effect, all things are quiescent and equal in a single suchness. To observe them through deluded vision is to perceive dualistic marks;
yet if one illuminates them with the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, they are like empty space, and no marks whatsoever can be apprehended.
Good son, it is only those bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts;

yet they do not seek to extinguish these deluded minds. They abide within the realm of deluded perceptions without adding any further cognitive discernment, and within this lack of discernment, they do not attempt to differentiate what is real.

This demonstrates the subtlety of the mind at peace in equality. As stated above, the distinctions of high and low status and the stages of realization exist only because one fails to understand the essence of the quiescent mind, falsely engaging in cultivation and realization while failing to let go of the duality of subject and object.
Although there are degrees of awakening, this now reveals the equality of the single mind, which spontaneously accords with the Way; this is perfect awakening.
This is the subtle principle of sudden realization. It holds that the daily activities and present experiences of all sentient beings are entirely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
If not a single thought arises, the whole body manifests spontaneously; thus it is said: "At all times, one must not intentionally give rise to deluded thoughts.
This is because the moment a single thought arises, one immediately becomes deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This refers to the delusion of sentient beings.

Thoughts are originally devoid of self-nature; they are fundamentally the true mind. If one were to cease delusion to seek the truth, it would be like cutting off one's head and seeking to remain alive.

Therefore, it is said: "Do not even attempt to extinguish these various deluded minds. This is because the realm of discursive thought is fundamentally the one true reality and admits of no deliberation.
To further apply a mind of conscious understanding would be like raising a shout to stop an echo. Therefore, it is said:
Abiding in the realm of delusive thoughts, one does not apply further discernment; this state of non-application is itself true knowledge.
If one gives rise to the mind to further discriminate and seek a separate reality, it is like placing a head upon a head, only increasing one's delusion.
Therefore, it is said: "In the absence of discerning knowledge, do not discriminate a reality. This is the secret method for settling the mind in daily life for the practitioner. If one can...
Spontaneously functioning in this manner, every thought merges with the Way and every moment realizes the Truth.
Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests the work of saving sentient beings. Among the patriarchs of the past, there has never been one who did not enter this Dharma-gate.
This is the upward path of Zen inquiry, what is called the "nose-ring of the patch-robed monk."
When those sentient beings hear this Dharma-gate, they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, giving rise to no fear or alarm;
this is what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.
This direct pointing to sudden enlightenment for settling the mind is the essential core of spiritual practice. This Dharma-gate is situated above [all others].
At all times and in all respects, this Dharma is difficult to believe, difficult to understand, and difficult to uphold.
If, upon hearing it, one does not give rise to alarm or fear, one may be said to be well able to accord with the nature of awakening.
"Good sons, you should know that such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
as well as to great Bodhisattvas, planting the roots of all virtues. The Buddha says that such a person is called one who has accomplished all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
This concludes the section on the mechanism of sudden enlightenment, which spontaneously accords with the Way.

Only those whose past causes and conditions are profound are able to believe and accept this without doubt. Although such individuals occupy the stage of a cause, they will certainly attain Buddhahood without question.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Pure Wisdom, you should know: The nature of perfect enlightenment Is without grasping and without realization;
There is neither bodhisattva nor sentient being. This verse shows that the nature of awakening is equal, fundamentally without distinction."
There is a gradual distinction between the time of awakening and the time before awakening.
Sentient beings are hindered by their lack of understanding, while Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended their conceptualization. Upon entering the stages, they attain eternal quiescence;
abiding in no signs, their great awakening is fully perfected—this is called "universal compliance."
The first two lines provide a general summary of the reasons for these distinctions. The phrase "sentient beings" refers to the stage of Identity in Practice (*xing-jie*).

The phrase "bodhisattvas" refers to the stage of Counterfeit Identity (*xiang-si-jie*). The two lines concerning "entering the stages" summarize the stage of Partially True Identity (*fen-zhen-jie*). The two lines concerning "Great Enlightenment" summarize the stage of Ultimate Identity (*jui-jing-jie*).
Furthermore, the initial line regarding "enlightened" and "unenlightened" also encompasses the stages of Identity in Principle (*li-jie*) and Identity in Name (*ming-zi-jie*).
If sentient beings in the final age do not give rise to delusion in their minds, the Buddha says that such people are Bodhisattvas in the present life;
they have already made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and their merit is fully perfected.
Although there are many skillful means, they are all termed "conformable wisdom."
The final two lines provide a general summary: although the stages and practices differ, they all accord with the nature of enlightenment.

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have extensively analyzed for us such accordance with the nature of awakening,
enabling all Bodhisattvas to receive the radiance of the awakened mind through the Buddha’s perfect voice, thereby attaining excellent benefit without depending on further cultivation."

This is a celebration of having heard the praise and expression of gratitude. Having heard the Buddha’s perfect voice, the light of the great wisdom teachings it flows forth has drenched the hearts of the great assembly.
Empowered by his spiritual power, their ignorance was shattered, and the luminosity of each individual's own mind suddenly manifested.
This is why they attained such excellent benefit without relying on gradual cultivation. Below follows the request for the expedient means to enter the gate.
World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates; those who come from the various directions do not arrive by only one path.
Likewise, all bodhisattvas’ adornment of buddha-lands and their attainment of bodhi do not rely on a single expedient means.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim for us all the expedient means and their gradual stages, as well as how many types there are in total for those who practice, so as to enable this...
This will cause Bodhisattvas and those in the final age who seek the Mahāyāna to swiftly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s ocean of great nirvāṇa.
This question concerns practice. Thus far, one has merely heard of the distinctions among what is realized, but has not yet heard of the practice that realizes it.
Therefore, I now specifically request the skillful means for entering the gate. The city is a metaphor for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*);
the gate is a metaphor for the path by which one enters. Skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely the practice for attaining realization;

it is the initial skillful means of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, what is called "taking advantage according to the direction," which constitutes the foundational work of practice. Regarding the "gradual stages": first is perfect illumination, and second...
[The Master] said: "Because this is the causal ground for attaining Buddhahood, it is first stated that 'knowing these to be empty flowers, there is no further transmigration.

To know the illusory and thereby depart from it without employing expedient means is the practice of sudden enlightenment through perfect cultivation; thus, no expedients are required. This is the conduct of those with the highest faculties.
Now, for the sake of those with middling and lower faculties, he requests the gradual sequence, the intent of which is to open the gates of the three contemplations. Thus it begins.
Having placed the order, one again practices the twenty-five wheels until they are perfected; all of these are gradual.
Having spoken these words, one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground. Thus one makes this request three times, beginning again from the end after each completion.
This passage describes the earnest sincerity of the quest for the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
It is well that you are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means. You should now listen attentively..."
"Listen; I shall speak for you.
Having thus granted permission and exhorted them to listen, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vaśitāprabhāsa, along with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence.
This is the joy of receiving the sound of the Dharma; it is the silent mind waiting in expectation to listen. The formal instruction follows:
"Good son, the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades all ten directions. It gives birth to the Tathāgatas and is of one essence and equal to all phenomena.
Regarding all practices, there is truly no duality."
This demonstrates that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is perfect and primordially devoid of delusion or enlightenment; it is equal and non-dual.
One merely accords with the single reality (*eka-tattva*) without relying on manifold practices. Therefore, it is said: "In all practices, there is truly no duality."
The skillful means that accord with [this] are immeasurable in number. To fully encompass what is returned to, according to the distinctions of nature, there should be three types;
these are the gates for correctly entering and realizing [enlightenment]. However, since the nature of awakening pervades all phenomena, then every phenomenon...
All are gates for entering into realization; they merely encompass all capacities according to individual circumstances, yet each possesses its essential core.

Therefore, there are only three gates. These three gates are precisely the three contemplations of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*upāya*), and the middle (*madhyama*). Furthermore, the enumeration of these three names is identical in both sutras.
In the Sanskrit language, they are called *śamatha*, *samāpatti*, and *dhyāna*. Regarding the ancient explanation of *śamatha*...
*Samatha* (mo ta) is translated here as "cessation" (*zhi*). Its characteristic is tranquility; its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

*Samāpatti* (san mo bo ti) is translated as "attainment" (*deng zhi*); it is also called *samādhi*. Its characteristic is illusory transformation; its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*).

*Dhyāna* (chan na) is translated as "meditative concentration" (*jing lu*). It is free from both tranquility and illusion; its characteristic is quiescent extinction. Its lower meaning corresponds to the Middle Way.

Contemplation. However, the reason one must necessarily employ the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) for cultivation and realization is that the *tathāgatagarbha* mind is endowed with the principle of the three truths (*trisatya*):
namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-emptiness, and both emptiness and non-emptiness. By means of these three contemplations, each illuminates one truth while collectively encompassing the single mind;

therefore, it is called "perfect illumination" (*pariniṣpanna-prakāśa*). Because the single mind illuminates perfectly, it is termed "sudden" (*tadana*); because the three contemplations illuminate sequentially, they are termed [gradual].
Gradual [cultivation]. In reality, there is fundamentally no difference in the sequence of three stages. This will be clarified later in the text. First, *śamatha*:
"Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment..."
This indicates the fundamental basis of practice; it is cultivation that accords with the nature after awakening, not cultivation within delusion.
That is to say, a bodhisattva’s practice must first involve the realization of the primordially existent, pure, and perfect true mind. Based upon this unborn and undying true mind, one practices.

One establishes contemplative practice to purify the habitual tendencies of ignorance accumulated over kalpas; this constitutes cultivation. It is solely in reference to being in accord with the nature that it is called cultivation.
Taking the pure awakened mind as the basis, one takes stillness as the practice. By clarifying all discursive thoughts, one perceives the agitation of consciousness, and tranquil wisdom arises.
The adventitious dust of body and mind is forever extinguished from this point on;
this demonstrates the characteristics of the practice of the contemplation of emptiness. One who awakens their initial resolve takes stillness as the foremost priority.

Because prior to awakening one was consistently distracted by deluded thoughts and agitation, now that this mind has been awakened, one should initiate [the practice] with the very mind of awakening thus realized.
Contemplate and observe. Reflect back upon the unmoving essence of the mind; therefore, it is said that taking stillness as one's practice.
Through this, delusive thoughts subside, and one perceives the signs of the arising and ceasing of habitual tendencies within the *ālayavijñāna*.

Therefore, it is said that by clarifying all thoughts, one awakens from the agitation of consciousness. If one observes for a long time, the luminosity of one's own mind will suddenly manifest. Thus...
It is said that stillness gives rise to wisdom. When the light of the mind flashes forth once, one suddenly perceives that body and mind are illusory and false, fundamentally non-existent;
thus they are like adventitious dust. In this way, one is internally liberated from body and mind, which is why it is called "eternal extinction.
This is the initial practice: the sudden realization of non-arising in a single thought-moment.

He is then able to internally give rise to tranquil pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear within it, like reflections in a mirror.

This demonstrates the efficacy of entering contemplation. Because the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-citta*) was previously obscured by the ignorance of the illusory and delusive body and mind, now that the body and mind have been liberated, the heavy burden of ignorance has ceased and vanished;

hence it is said, "Internally, tranquility and lightness arise. Upon reaching this state where the ten directions are vast and open, the originally existing *dharmakāya* emerges clearly; hence it is said:

The hearts of all Tathāgatas manifest like reflections in a mirror; that is to say, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature, and my mind in turn merges with the Tathāgata, thereby wondrously harmonizing with the Dharma-body.
This is precisely the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* of reversing the flow and returning to the single source, where the six faculties cease their activity.
The lands of the ten directions become brilliantly pure, like a piece of lapis lazuli suspended within.
The bright moon—indeed, all Tathāgatas, secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous—manifest within it.
This corresponds to the sudden penetration of the marks of ignorance according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
This skillful means is called *śamatha*; this is its formal designation.
*Śamatha* translates as "cessation" (*zhi*), meaning tranquility. When referring to the cause, it is called cessation; when referring to the fruit, it is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness.
Next is samāpatti. Good son,
if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment,
they take that awakened mind of pure, perfect enlightenment as the foundation for their practice.
With a mind of pure awakening, one realizes that the nature of the mind, as well as the faculties and their objects, are all produced by illusion.

Thereupon, one gives rise to various illusions to eliminate the perceiver of illusion; by transforming these illusions, one opens the way for the assembly of illusory beings. Because these illusions are thus aroused, one is able to inwardly give rise to great compassion and tranquility.
This demonstrates the characteristics of the provisional contemplation (*jia guan*). "Mind-nature" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This means that, based on the awakened mind of pure, perfect enlightenment (*viśuddha-pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*), one gives rise to the illumination of wisdom (*jñāna-āloka*) to illuminate that consciousness, along with the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). One sees that these are fundamentally non-existent; they are all manifestations produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Although they appear to exist, their nature is eternally empty of itself. Therefore, it is said that they are all due to illusory transformations (*māyā-vikāra*). Now, as for these illusory transformations...

This refers to the ignorance at the tips of the branches. Once one has realized that one’s own consciousness, as well as the sense organs and their objects, are all like illusions and transformations, one then analogically contemplates all sentient beings, seeing each and every one as being like an illusion.
Thus it is said: "One immediately gives rise to various illusions to eliminate the illusory agent.
Here, "various illusions" refers to illusory wisdom; this "illusory agent" refers to the fundamental ignorance. This means relying on the beginningless [ignorance] which is like an illusion.

The wisdom of awakening suddenly shatters fundamental ignorance. Regarding "transformation" and so forth: it means that once ignorance is extinguished, inconceivable karmic functions arise spontaneously;

thus it is said that one manifests various illusions and opens up for illusory multitudes, extensively performing the Buddha-work of saving sentient beings by manifesting bodies within the ten realms to universally respond to all.
This describes the process of emerging from the true and entering the conventional.

This is the aspect of practice. Regarding "arising from illusion and so forth," it means that having already realized *tathatā* (suchness), one initiates activities for the benefit of sentient beings arising from that suchness;
yet, through great compassion of identical essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*), one extensively transforms sentient beings without grasping at the marks of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "the great compassion of pliancy."

All Bodhisattvas initiate their practice from this point and gradually advance. Because that observer of illusions is not identical to the illusion, yet because all things—including the non-illusory observation—are themselves illusory, the characteristics of illusion are forever extinguished.

This demonstrates the signs of progress in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Because the realization of the nature has not yet reached perfection and ignorance has not yet been purified, one enters deeper and deeper;
hence it is called "gradual. Because dualistic opposition has not yet been forgotten, one first eliminates the object of contemplation while the subject—the wisdom that contemplates—still remains;
hence it is said, "The one who contemplates the illusion is not identical to the illusion. "The one who contemplates the illusion" refers to the contemplator.
The "ability to observe" is the wisdom; the "illusion" is the object observed. Since true wisdom alone remains, it is not the same as that illusion.
However, since the object observed is illusory, the observing subject also vanishes. If the observing subject still persists, one has not yet escaped from illusion.

Therefore, it is said that this is not the same as the contemplation of illusion; for since all things are illusory, both subject and object are forgotten, and both the objective realm and wisdom are transcended.
There remains only the single true mind; thus it is said that "illusory appearances are forever departed."
This is the perfected and wondrous practice of these Bodhisattvas. It is like grain growing from soil;

this is a metaphor for the aspect of progressive advancement. That is to say, when a Bodhisattva’s contemplative practice reaches the point where both object and wisdom are forgotten and the single reality stands alone, then the true ground of the Dharmakāya becomes the fertile soil in which the spiritual sprouts of the seeds of wisdom gradually grow. The "soil" is a metaphor for the true Dharmakāya.
The ground is like the seed of original enlightenment and true suchness (*tathatā*); the increasing clarity of contemplative wisdom is like the growth of sprouts.
This skillful means is called *samāpatti*. This is the name for the culmination of contemplation.
In Sanskrit, *samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium" (*děngzhì*). Within the context of meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), it refers to this state.
Because they are able to reach the stage of the sages.
Third is *dhyāna*.
Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment,
This is the fundamental practice:
with a mind of pure awakening, do not grasp at illusory transformations or any signs of purity. Realize that both body and mind are hindrances;
through the clarity of non-cognitive awareness, do not rely on any obstacles. Thus, you will forever transcend the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction, and enjoy the world.
As for the body and mind, their characteristics exist within the realm of sensory objects, like the resonance of a bell within a vessel that issues forth externally;
thus, afflictions and nirvana do not obstruct or hinder one another.
This precisely demonstrates the characteristics of the Middle Way practice, meaning that one establishes contemplation based upon the awakened mind of pure, perfect *bodhi*.
Practice. Directly contemplate the Middle Way with single-mindedness. Because one externally forgets the objective realm, it is said that "one does not grasp at illusory transformations.

Internally, one forgets wisdom and does not grasp at the mark of stillness. When both realm and wisdom are forgotten, body and mind are quiescent and extinguished, and there is no obstruction whatsoever;

thus it is said that "one thoroughly knows. This "knowing" is luminous awareness, which is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). This means that once all oppositions are forgotten, the subject and object...

If it does not stand, then ignorance is purified and exhausted; thus it is said that there is no cognition of clarity. Since both object and wisdom are empty, it is said that it does not rely on any obstructions.
Because it is detached from objects, it transcends obstruction; because it is detached from wisdom, it transcends non-obstruction.

Being ultimately quiescent and extinguished, it is said that it has forever attained transcendence. *Huang* refers to the sound of bells and drums; although they possess a physical substance, [the resonance]—
It is not that sound is obstructed from reaching afar; rather, it is precisely because the vessel is subtle that the sound is great.

This clarifies that even at a point of obstruction, one can reach through without hindrance. The meaning is this: as long as the mind and its objects have not been forgotten, the body, mind, and world act as obstructions.
Now, having realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), these very illusory and false body, mind, and world do not obstruct the Dharma-body; therefore, it is called "enjoyment" (*paribhoga*).
The world, as well as the body and mind, exist within the realm of sensory objects like a sound resonating from a bell inside a vessel;
this serves as a metaphor for the Dharma-body emerging from obstruction. "Afflictions" refers to the phenomena of birth and death, namely the body, mind, and world.
"Nirvana" refers to wisdom and principle, because it is solely the true mind. Thus, birth and death and nirvana do not obstruct or hinder one another.

One is then able to internally give rise to the tranquility of quiescent extinction (*śānti-praśrabdhi*). This wondrous awakening accords with the realm of quiescent extinction, which cannot be reached by the body or mind of oneself or others;
the lives and spans of sentient beings are all but floating thoughts.

This demonstrates the signs of the benefits achieved through the completion of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Since birth and death have been extinguished and quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) has manifested before one, the three virtues are perfectly realized, and there is the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*;

hence it is called "quiescence and light ease. As every thought-moment accords with wondrous enlightenment and quiescent extinction, it is said that "it cannot be reached by the body or mind of self or others. Sentient beings and their lifespans are all merely floating [phenomena].
Contemplation. This is the eternal severance of the two obstacles and the eternal forgetting of the two deaths; it is what is called the ultimate realization of the single mind.
This skillful means is named *dhyāna*.
This is the name of these knots.

Good son, these three dharma-gates are all in close proximity to and in accord with Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). It is because of these that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Buddhahood;
and the various skillful means, including all their similarities and differences, of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, all rely upon these three.
These various practices, if fully realized, constitute Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
This is a summary of the gradual stages of the skillful means (*upāya*).

That is to say, these three dharma-gates are all skillful means for accords with and approaches Perfect Enlightenment; they are the ground of the Tathāgata’s practice and the myriad deeds of the Bodhisattvas. Or...
Whether gradual or sudden, whether partial or complete, all rely upon these three kinds of practice—whether cultivated singly, in combination, or in a perfect synthesis.
If one realizes them perfectly in a single thought-moment, one immediately attains Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
"Good son, suppose there were someone who cultivates the noble path and brings to fruition the fruits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of arhats and pratyekabuddhas;
this would not equal a person who, upon hearing this unimpeded Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment,
practices it accordingly for even a single kṣaṇa."
This passage clarifies the superiority of this practice. For the cultivation of the partial and the perfect [vehicles] differs by factors of ten million and a kalpa respectively;
thus, it is not as good to teach many followers of the Two Vehicles as it is for them to hear this Dharma even briefly, for it is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
He then restated it again in verse:
"O Mahātejas, you should know: The mind of the Unsurpassed Great Enlightenment Is, from its primordial limit, devoid of dual characteristics."
The various skillful means that accord with [the truth] are immeasurable in number; the Tathāgata has summarized and revealed them as being of three types.
This general verse establishes three kinds of contemplative practice.
Quiescent śamatha is like a mirror reflecting all images;
The illusory-like samādhi is like a sprout gradually growing; Dhyāna is solely cessation, Like the decorative rings within a vessel.
This verse describes three types of aspects of practice.
These three kinds of sublime Dharma gates are all in accord with awakening;

it is by means of them that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas attain the Way upon the causal ground. Because these three matters are perfectly realized, this concludes the summary verse that establishes the title.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśvabhāṣin rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
At the outset, he asked about the proper conduct for approaching [the Buddha]:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, such a Dharma-gate is truly rare;
I offer my praise."
"World-Honored One, regarding these various skillful means, how many ways of cultivation are there for all bodhisattvas within the gateway of Perfect Enlightenment?
This is the precise intent of the question being posed. It refers to the three contemplations previously taught by the Buddha;

it is not yet known whether a single person possesses all three, or whether three people each possess one, or whether they are practiced simultaneously or sequentially. Therefore, he requests an elucidation.
This is for the purpose of cultivation.
I pray that you will provide skillful instruction for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the future age, enabling them to realize the true nature of reality.
This is the intent behind this inquiry.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again, manifesting his utmost sincerity on three occasions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇaghoṣa, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O son of good family, you..."
He is able to act for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the final age who inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation.
Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Having been exhorted to speak,
the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin, together with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence,
waiting expectantly.
"Good son, all Tathāgatas are perfectly awakened and pure; fundamentally, there is neither cultivation nor one who cultivates.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, however, cultivate based on the power of illusion arising from non-awakening.
At that time, there arise twenty-five kinds of wheels of pure meditative concentration."
This is the general response to the intent of the question. The pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment is inherently possessed by all sentient beings and does not depend upon cultivation.
However, because they currently abide within delusion, they cultivate the illusory with the illusory; it is solely due to the power of this illusion that twenty-five different types arise.
For the three contemplations within the single mind are fundamentally without distinction; it is only that each person, according to their own inclination, emphasizes one aspect over the others.
The practices are developed sequentially to form twenty-five wheels; however, it is not that there are definitively twenty-five distinct types.

Rather, these twenty-five types do not transcend the three contemplations (trivipassanā); they are differentiated according to whether they are practiced singly, in combination, or in a complete, integrated manner. Initially, one practices the three contemplations individually.
If a bodhisattva takes up only extreme tranquility and, by the power of that tranquility, permanently severs the afflictions and achieves ultimate perfection,
entering nirvana without rising from their seat, this bodhisattva is said to be one who practices śamatha alone.

This refers to the single cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). However, since the three truths (*tri-satya*) are fundamentally one and the same object, the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*) are rooted in a single mind.
They are perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive; to mention one is to possess all three, and to speak of the three is to realize their essence as one.

This is because they are respectively the "correct" (the Middle Way), the "partial" (emptiness), and the "combined" (provisionality). Thus, although one may cultivate a single contemplation, it necessarily encompasses the other two; even if not explicitly stated, this meaning is fully present.
[The preceding] is complete. Now, it is said that one takes only the ultimate stillness; therefore, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is primary.

By the power of this stillness, one eternally severs the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, the meaning encompasses the provisional (*prajñapti*). Since the afflictions are illusory transformations, they are severed by the power of stillness.
If one achieves the ultimate and perfectly realizes the single mind (*ekacitta*), then the middle [truth] is subsumed. Therefore, without rising from one's seat, one enters *nirvāṇa*.

"Pan. This [title] refers solely to entering by means of the solitary, perfect cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). To be able to perform such contemplation, the meaning is only then fulfilled.
The title should have been "Awakening to Pure Perfect Enlightenment" (*Awu Jing Yuanjue*); the translator has merely abbreviated it.
If bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, yet— by the power of the Buddha—

perform the various activities of transforming worlds and fully practice the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva, they shall not lose their tranquil mindfulness or their various subtle wisdoms regarding dhāraṇīs.
This Bodhisattva practices *samāpatti* exclusively; this refers to the exclusive cultivation of the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*).
As for "the power of the Buddha," it refers to the power of internal perfuming by the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the Buddha-nature, which is inherently possessed by one's own nature;
thus, various transformative functions are initiated, and one fully cultivates sublime practices. This is based on illusion (*māyā*).
In practicing the dhāraṇī, if one does not lose the state of tranquil mindfulness, then the entire substance gives rise to its function.

This simultaneously encompasses the substance of the Middle Way’s quiescence within the single mind, giving rise to the wisdom of emptiness that illuminates and shatters ignorance; thus, the provisional encompasses the emptiness within the middle.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions without engaging in activity, and sever the afflictions alone such that, once the afflictions are completely severed,
they realize the true mark, these bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* exclusively.

This is the single cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). By merely extinguishing all illusions and exclusively severing afflictions (*kleśa*), one gathers the provisional into the Middle;
when afflictions are completely severed, one ascends to the true reality (*dharmatā*), thereby gathering emptiness into the Middle.

Thus, cessation and illumination are simultaneous, manifesting the Middle. Because it exclusively extinguishes and exhausts [afflictions], it is a dual negation; because it exclusively severs and realizes [the truth], it is a dual affirmation.
[Zhao] comments: The above constitutes the single cultivation of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). Below follows the combined cultivation of the twenty-one wheels (*ekaviṃśati-cakra*).

Each contemplation governs seven [wheels], hence there are twenty-one. First, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) governs seven. Within this, the first two contemplations are cultivated in combination.
First emptiness, then the provisional.
If bodhisattvas first attain ultimate stillness and, with a mind of tranquil wisdom, illuminate all illusions, they will then, within that state, [perceive them as such].
They give rise to the bodhisattva practice. Such a bodhisattva is said to first cultivate śamatha and subsequently cultivate samāpatti;
next, they first cultivate emptiness and subsequently the middle way.
If these bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of ultimate stillness, they will then sever the afflictions and forever transcend birth and death.
This Bodhisattva first cultivates *śamatha* and subsequently cultivates *dhyāna*.

Because this is the wisdom that takes the essence as its substance, it is called "tranquil wisdom" (*jinghui*). As it illuminates back toward the tranquil essence, it is called "realizing the nature of ultimate stillness.
Thereby, afflictions are severed, and one eternally transcends birth and death; cause and effect both vanish, and one perfectly realizes the single mind. Therefore, this is the Middle Way.
Next, one further contemplates these two through three stages:
first emptiness, then the provisional, and finally the middle.
If bodhisattvas, by means of quiescent wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver all sentient beings.
Subsequently, he severed all afflictions and entered into nirvana. This bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, next cultivated *samāpatti*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.
Next, first emptiness, then the middle, and finally the provisional.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate tranquility, have severed the afflictions, they subsequently give rise to the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva.
To deliver all sentient beings: this Bodhisattva first cultivates *śamatha*, then cultivates *dhyāna*, and subsequently cultivates *samāpatti*.
Next, they cultivate the three contemplations in equal measure. First, through stillness, they bring the illusory to rest and quiescence.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of ultimate tranquility, sever the afflictions with their minds, further deliver sentient beings, and establish worlds,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated śamatha and then practiced samāpatti and dhyāna in equal measure.
Next, first one quiets the illusion and afterwards attains stillness.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, first give rise to transformations and subsequently sever the afflictions, such bodhisattvas—
This is called first practicing *śamatha* and *samāpatti*, and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*.
It is like first attaining stillness and silence, and subsequently manifesting illusions.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, employ it to support quiescent extinction, they subsequently give rise to activity and transform the world.
This Bodhisattva is named Qiuxiu; he first cultivates śamatha-dhyāna and subsequently cultivates samāpatti.
Having completed the seven wheels of the superior contemplation of stillness, he now proceeds to the seven wheels of the lower contemplation of illusion.
First there is illusion, and subsequently stillness.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, adapt in various ways and thereby attain ultimate stillness, such bodhisattvas—
This is called first practicing *samāpatti* and subsequently practicing *śamatha*;
next, first the illusory and subsequently the quiescent.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, takes various realms as the basis for attaining cessation, such a bodhisattva—
This is called first practicing *samāpatti* and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*.
In the former, one repeats the second; in the latter, one repeats the third.
Initially there is illusion, followed by stillness, and finally quiescence.
If bodhisattvas perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abide in tranquility, and sever the afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated samāpatti, then cultivated śamatha, and finally cultivated dhyāna.
Next, there is first illusion, then tranquility, and finally stillness.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions, they abide in ultimate stillness.
This Bodhisattva first cultivates samāpatti, then cultivates dhyāna, and finally cultivates śamatha; subsequently, he brings these three contemplations into equilibrium.
First, there is the illusory, then stillness, and finally quiescence.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation and skillful means, reach tranquil extinction while remaining compliant with both,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti* and then cultivated *śamatha* and *dhyāna* in equal measure.
Next comes sameness, followed by illusion, stillness, and finally quiescence.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, employ various manifestations to support ultimate stillness, they subsequently sever the afflictions.
This Bodhisattva is named "Equal Cultivation of Samāpatti and Śamatha, followed by Cultivation of Dhyāna.
Afterward, they equalize illusion and stillness, and subsequently quietude.
If these Bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, support their state of cessation (nirvāṇa), they subsequently abide in pure, effortless meditative concentration (dhyāna).
This Bodhisattva is named Qi (Equal): he first cultivates samāpatti-dhyāna and subsequently cultivates śamatha.
He possesses the sevenfold mastery of the three types of tranquil contemplation, and within that duality, there are two further pairs.
First quiescence, then stillness.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to supreme stillness and abide in purity, such bodhisattvas—
It is said that one first cultivates dhyāna and subsequently cultivates śamatha;
first stillness and subsequently illusion.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to functional activity, they accord with both stillness and function regarding all objects.
This Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates dhyāna and subsequently cultivates samāpatti. Furthermore, there are two further categories:
first, initial stillness; second, subsequent tranquility; and finally, the illusory.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*) and through various intrinsic natures, abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *dhyāna*, then cultivated *śamatha*, and finally cultivated *samāpatti*.
Next is first quiescence (*śama*), then illusion (*māyā*), and finally tranquility (*praśama*).
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation and the unconditioned nature (*anabhisaṃskāra-svabhāva*), give rise to activity within the pure realm (*viśuddha-gocara*).
They return to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This Bodhisattva is said to first cultivate *dhyāna*, then cultivate *samāpatti*, and finally cultivate *śamatha*.
Later, they bring the three realms into equilibrium; first, they pacify and align the illusions through stillness.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation and through various forms of purity, abide in meditative concentration and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated dhyāna and practiced śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure.
Next, following the samādhi of tranquility, there is the illusion-like state.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, support ultimate stillness and give rise to transformations, such bodhisattvas—
It is called "Equal Cultivation" when one first cultivates *śamatha* and subsequently cultivates *samāpatti*.
It is called "Subsequent Equalization" when, after the illusory [nature of phenomena] has been stilled, one subsequently attains tranquility.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*nirodha*), augment their transformative powers (*nirmāṇa*) and give rise to the wisdom of the most profound stillness and luminous clarity.
This Bodhisattva is named "Simultaneous Cultivation of Dhyāna and Samāpatti, Followed by the Cultivation of Śamatha.
Subsequently, they perfectly cultivate the three contemplations.

If these Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unify all things, then regarding all natures and characteristics, there is nothing that departs from the nature of enlightenment.
This Bodhisattva is said to be one who has perfectly cultivated the three kinds of self-nature purity in accordance with reality.
This perfect cultivation of the three contemplations is, in fact, the three contemplations within a single mind, complete in a single thought-moment.

This is what was first called "perfectly illuminating the aspect of pure awakening. When perfect awakening is perfectly unified, it then universally illuminates all things, thereby encompassing the ten dharma realms. Regarding this:
The characteristics of all natures do not depart from the nature of awakening; they are the very marks of pure awakening.

In the original ground of the Buddhas' initial practice, there is only the single mind’s perfect illumination of the Dharma-realm, which constitutes their sublime conduct. Thus, the twenty-five wheels ultimately converge upon this.
This intends to show that this single contemplation is the complete cultivation, while the other twenty-four merely follow according to individual faculties.
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva. All bodhisattvas practice in this manner.
If any bodhisattvas or sentient beings of the final age rely upon these wheels, they should maintain pure conduct and engage in tranquil contemplation."
Seek compassion through repentance for twenty-one days. Place markers at each of the twenty-five wheels and seek compassion with a sincere heart.

As you grasp them with your hand, observe the knots formed; according to the indications of these knots, one will immediately know whether the path is sudden or gradual. If there is even a single moment of doubt or regret, success will not be achieved.

Now, to experience joy or anger upon hearing praise or blame is precisely because this joy and anger are rooted in the mark of self (*ātman*).
It is not Nirvāṇa. By this one may verify that such a person firmly clings to the mark of self; by means of this seed...
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) lies latent; when it encounters objects, it manifests as active states (pravṛttivijñāna), playing through the various sense faculties without ever ceasing.
If one seeks the Way by means of this, how can liberation be attained?
"Good son, those who cultivate the Way do not eliminate the mark of self; therefore, they cannot enter pure awakening.
This is a summary of the fault of seeking the Way while clinging to a self.
The following passage reveals the source of the illness:
"Good son, if one knows the emptiness of the self, there is no one who can destroy the self. When I preach the Dharma, it is because my 'self' has not yet been severed.
It is the same for sentient beings, life-span, and so forth."
This uses the Dharma to test for illness; conversely, it reveals that the mark of self (*ātman*) has not yet been forgotten. Now, Nirvana is the Dharma of emptiness.
If one were to truly realize Nirvana, then the mark of self would necessarily be empty. If the mark of self were empty, how could there be praise or blame?
That one now gives rise to joy or anger because of praise or blame directed at this Dharma is precisely the sign that the mark of self has not been severed. If I...
If the marks have not yet been severed, then the four marks of persons, sentient beings, life-span, and self-nature remain fully present.
This is precisely the root of the sickness of sentient beings; how, then, could this be considered the attainment of nirvana?
The following correctly demonstrates the source of the illness:
"Good son, the sentient beings of the final age explain illness as being the Dharma; for this reason, they are called those who are to be pitied.
Although they apply themselves with diligent effort, they only increase their various illnesses; therefore, they are unable to enter pure awakening."
This correctly indicates the source of the illness. It means that practitioners of the Dharma in the末代 (final age) have not yet severed the mark of self (*ātman*).
Because they mistake the self for the Dharma, what they preach is merely the preaching of the illness of their own marks of self, rather than the teaching of the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is said that "they preach the illness as the Dharma. For this reason, although they practice with diligence, it only increases [their afflictions].
This further aggravates various illnesses; therefore, they are unable to enter pure awakening. For this reason, they are called "those who are to be pitied.
(The following demonstrates the faults of clinging to illness.
"Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks. Taking the understanding of the Tathāgata and his sphere of practice as..."
If one practices by oneself, one will ultimately not achieve success.

This demonstrates the fault of taking the illness of attachment as the Dharma. It means that a practitioner who does not understand the four marks (the four phases of existence) merely takes the Tathāgata’s understanding and practice as their own;
because it is not their own direct realization, they will ultimately not achieve success.
There may be sentient beings who, not having attained, claim to have attained; not having realized, claim to have realized. Upon seeing those who have made superior progress, they give rise to envy.
Because such beings have not severed the view of self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
This demonstrates the fault of clinging to such a sickness. One will inevitably fall into the category of those possessed by overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
In reality, one has neither attained nor realized anything, yet one claims for oneself that it has been realized and attained; being satisfied with a mere trifle, this constitutes overweening pride.

This is precisely the case for those who have not severed self-love (*ātmasneha*). How is this known? It is because they give rise to envy and jealousy toward those who see superior progress. However, this...
The mind of jealousy arises from self-love; therefore, one knows that such a person has not yet severed self-love.
For this reason, they are unable to enter pure awakening. This is a profound statement regarding how self-love is the root of all illness.
The following is an admonition regarding the investigation of transgressions:
"Good son, when sentient beings in the final age desire to achieve the Way, do not allow them to seek awakening merely for the sake of increasing their learning,
which only serves to augment their views of self."

This is a profound admonition to guard against transgressions. It means that for those who cling to illness as being the Dharma, the reason the four marks [of existence] have not been eliminated is simply because they take the single matter of "waiting for enlightenment" as the root of their ailment.

If one harbors a mind that waits for enlightenment, one will inevitably seek out scriptures and teachings extensively, clinging to superficial words and turning them into one's own interpretations; therefore, this is merely...
This increases one's erudition but grows one's view of self; it is not true cultivation. How can those who aspire to the Way in the Dharma-ending age not be fearful?
One should simply apply oneself with diligence to subdue the afflictions and give rise to great valor, so that what has not been attained may be attained and what has not been severed may be severed.
Greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, and envy do not arise toward their objects; attachment to self and others is entirely extinguished.
The Buddha says that such a person gradually achieves accomplishment, seeks out virtuous friends, and does not fall into false views.
This is an exhortation to authentic cultivation. A practitioner of authentic cultivation need not direct the mind toward awaiting enlightenment, nor need they extensively seek out much learning;
they should simply take the subduing of afflictions as their primary practice. Furthermore, one must not consider a small attainment to be sufficient;
regarding that which has not yet been attained—nirvana—one must be determined to attain it, and regarding those afflictions not yet severed, one must resolutely desire to sever them.
Simply examine the mind as it encounters various objects. When confronted with all afflictions such as greed, anger, attachment, and pride, do they truly fail to arise?
Furthermore, regarding self and other, and all forms of affection, do they truly become entirely quiescent?
Examine your own mind in this way; it is just as the ancient masters said: "In studying the Way, there is no need to seek awakening by exerting the mind; simply, within a single..."
To be able to penetrate through the sphere of all afflictions is the very place of awakening. Therefore, the Buddha said that such a person can gradually achieve accomplishment.
Nevertheless, one must further seek out a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to decisively distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, so as not to fall into false views.
Only by practicing in this manner will there be even a slight degree of correspondence with the truth.
"Can those who study not exert themselves?
If one harbors any seeking, giving rise to further hatred and attachment, then one cannot enter the ocean of pure awakening.
This is a renewed exhortation for true cultivation and a warning to remain free from transgressions. It means that one must act exactly as described above; only then is it true [cultivation]."
If one abandons this and separately gives rise to a mind of longing and aversion, grasping and rejecting, or hatred and love,
then one will ultimately be unable to enter pure awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Pure Karma, you should know that all sentient beings, due to grasping at a self and craving, have wandered through beginningless delusion;
because they have not eliminated the four kinds of marks, they cannot achieve Bodhi.
Love and hatred arise in their minds, and crookedness persists in their thoughts; for this reason, they are frequently bewildered and distressed.
One cannot enter the City of Awakening;
this city is a metaphor for nirvāṇa. It is said that this nirvāṇa cannot be invaded by Māras or externalists;
it is the gathering place of myriad virtues, the destination of all sages, and the entry point for all practices. Therefore, it is likened to a city.
If one can take refuge in awakening the realm, first eliminate greed, anger, and delusion; when attachment to dharmas no longer dwells in the mind, one may gradually achieve accomplishment.
Since my own body is fundamentally non-existent, from what cause could hatred or love arise?
Such a person seeks virtuous friends and will never fall into false views; as for what is sought, do not give rise to a separate mind.

The ultimate non-attainment of lands is the general designation for the world; it is also taken as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. Because the mind loves *nirvāṇa*, it is called "attachment to the Dharma" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
The remaining verses are easily understood.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Pujue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Jin asked about the rules of deportment:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have eloquently expounded upon the ailments of dhyāna, causing the great assembly to attain what they have never experienced before;
our minds are cleared and we have obtained great peace and stability."
[He] offered praise and gratitude:

"World-Honored One, in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha; the worthy and holy ones will remain hidden, while false teachings will blaze ever more fiercely.
What kind of person should these sentient beings seek? Upon what dharma should they rely? What practices should they perform? What illnesses should they eliminate? How [should they proceed]?"
He generates the resolve to ensure that those blind from birth do not fall into false views.
This correctly restates the question posed. This question has five parts: first, asking what kind of person one should seek; the answer below is that one seeks a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Second, asking by means of what dharma; third, asking by means of what practice; fourth, asking how to eliminate... [the text continues].
"What are the illnesses? These three questions provide a general answer: based on the Dharma that has been realized, one should avoid the four illnesses.
Regarding the fifth question, "How does one generate the mind [of awakening]? the generation of the vast and other types of minds is clarified in the subsequent text.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Thus they made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
Having thus displayed their utmost diligence three times, the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you all..."
You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such practice;
you are able to bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Path, enabling those beings to attain the Noble Way. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Having praised [the teaching] and exhorted them to listen, at that time the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the instruction and listened in silence.
As they waited expectantly for the response, there are five parts to the answer; first is the answer concerning the seeking of the person.

"Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve upon the Great Mind and seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in order to practice, they should seek one who possesses all correct knowledge and vision;
whose mind does not dwell on signs; who is not attached to the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

who, though manifesting amidst worldly afflictions, remains ever pure in mind; who displays the appearance of various faults yet praises the holy life (brahmacarya); and who does not cause sentient beings to enter [into error]."
One who lacks discipline seeks such a person and thereby achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This answers the question of what kind of person one should seek. A "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) is one who well knows the faculties of sentient beings, teaches the Dharma according to their capacity, diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine, and brings about peace and security.
One with right knowledge and vision is one whose mind does not dwell [on anything].

Regarding the characteristics: "One who does not cling to the practices of the two vehicles," though manifesting the six aspects such as worldly afflictions (*rajas*), describes the conduct of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Because the Bodhisattva dwells in the midst of the mundane without being defiled, it is said that "the mind is ever pure. This is through the means of gathering [beings] by means of commonality (*samānārthatā*).
Therefore, it is said that he manifests various faults; first, he entices them with the hook of desire, and afterwards, he causes them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thus, it is said that he does not allow sentient beings to enter into non-discipline. By seeking such a person, one will immediately achieve the unsurpassed right path.
Sentient beings of the final age who see such a person should provide offerings without regard for their own bodies or lives.
That spiritual friend constantly manifests purity throughout the four modes of conduct, even when manifesting various forms of faults and afflictions, yet their mind remains free from arrogance.

How much more so regarding the accumulation of wealth, wives, children, and kinsmen! If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward such a virtuous friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment;
the flower of his mind will radiate brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.

This is the methodological standard for serving a spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*). One should not begrudge one’s body or life, as exemplified by the Bodhisattva Śvetaparvata who sacrificed his body, Sadāprarudita who broke his own bones, and others who even offered their bodies as beds and seats.
To always manifest the four modes of conduct in purity is the way to follow a spiritual mentor;
therefore, one should serve them to the end of one's life. Even if there are instances of contrary behavior, they are merely skillful manifestations.
Regarding greed, anger, and delusion—such as in the cases of the woman Vāsuladattā or King Anavatapta—one would not dare to give rise to a mind of arrogance;
how much less so for grasping at food or wealth? "Grasping" (*bhojana*) refers to solid food, while "wealth" (*dhana*) refers to treasures.
The meaning is that if one does not even dare to be arrogant when internal greed and anger manifest, how much less so for external things such as solid food, wealth, wives, children, and retinues?
This belongs to the natural course of human existence, as exemplified by the case of Vimalakīrti; how, then, could one ever treat such a person with contempt?
If a practitioner does not give rise to malicious thoughts toward such a "contrary" spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), this is what is meant by "relying on the Dharma and not relying on the person."

One is thus able to achieve ultimate perfection. Having forever severed the root of doubt and possessing a direct mind and right mindfulness, the flower of the mind blossoms with radiance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
This concludes the answer to the question regarding the Dharma upon which one relies.
"Good son, the sublime Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should be free from the four illnesses.
This answers the question regarding the Dharma upon which one relies; the intent is to select a teacher—that is, to seek out a person of right knowledge and vision.
Practice relies on the Dharma, and the Dharma must rely on a teacher; therefore, one should rely only on a person of right knowledge and vision whom one has carefully selected. How so?"
Know that such a person possesses right knowledge and right view; simply test them by means of the Dharma. If the Dharma they teach involves the mind abiding in signs, it is a sickness of the Dharma.
If one is free from this sickness of the Dharma, then know that their knowledge and vision are inherently correct. Therefore, following the various patriarchs of antiquity—
To sever emotional attachments and remove fetters, there has never been a real dharma that binds people; this is what it means to be one who does not dwell in signs.
If this is so, then it may be relied upon.
What are the four illnesses? The first is the illness of fabrication. If there is someone who speaks thus: "Regarding my original mind..."

To perform various practices in the desire to seek perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-avabodha) is called a "sickness," because the nature of perfect enlightenment is not something to be attained through effort.
This explains the characteristics of the four sicknesses; this is the first, the sickness of effort. Now, as for why effort is a sickness:
the nature of perfect enlightenment is naturally and inherently possessed, requiring no artificial effort. To now seek perfect enlightenment through a cultivation based on effort is [the sickness].
One awakens to the wondrous nature. Now, how could this wondrous nature be sought through deliberate effort? Therefore, it is said to be a "disease.
