If there were someone who spoke such words, even if that person of knowledge were to speak them themselves.
Second is the illness of "indulgence. If there are those who speak thus: "We now neither sever birth-and-death nor seek nirvana;
we harbor no thought of arising or ceasing regarding nirvana or birth-and-death, but leave everything as it is, following the nature of all phenomena."
In seeking perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), that nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that exists by mere default; therefore, it is called a "sickness.
This demonstrates that being at ease [with the mind] is itself a sickness. However, this sickness of being at ease belongs to those of deluded understanding who indifferently follow their own nature.
They run wild with body and mind, claiming for themselves that they are unrestrained and unimpeded, having attained great liberation.
On the contrary, they use as a pretext that, fundamentally, there is no birth-and-death to be severed and no nirvana to be realized, using this as a justification for their indulgence;

such people do not possess true knowledge and vision, nor are they true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). If one relies upon such individuals, one will fall into arrogance and madness; therefore, it is said that [relying on them] is to follow one's own whims.
This is because it is a sickness.
Third is the sickness of cessation. If there is another person who speaks thus: "I shall now permanently cease all thoughts within my own mind and attain the quiescent equality of all natures;
I desire to seek Perfect Enlightenment," that nature of Perfect Enlightenment does not arise from the union with cessation.
This is called "sickness.
This indicates that cessation itself is the sickness. However, Perfect Enlightenment shines universally, and its great function is without fixed direction;
how could it be sought by permanently stilling all thoughts and indulging in the practice of withered stillness? For the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not...
It is merely that they are combined; therefore, it is said to be a "sickness.
Fourth is the sickness of cessation. If there is another person who says, "I have now permanently severed all afflictions," [this too is a sickness].
The body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent; how much more so are the sense organs, objects, and delusive realms? All are eternally quiescent.
To seek perfect enlightenment while holding such views is called a "sickness," for the nature of perfect enlightenment is not a state of mere quiescence.

This indicates that taking cessation as an illness is a delusion. The nature of enlightenment is perfect and complete; it manifests in accordance with conditions, being quiescent yet ever-illuminating.
Now, if one regards it as ultimately empty and non-existent, one nearly falls into nihilism. To seek perfect enlightenment through permanent extinction leads to a long-term stagnation;
to dwell in non-conceptualization causes one to fall into the stage of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, this is considered an illness.

"One who is free from the four ailments then knows purity. One who performs this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice false contemplation.

This concludes the demonstration of right contemplation. It begins by stating: "The mark of the perfectly illuminating, pure awakening" refers to the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Originally, these do not belong to the four states of effort, cessation, maintenance, and extinction. Now, by being free from these four, one’s own nature is perfectly luminous;
since it was originally without deficiency, it is called "pure. However, the four states such as effort and cessation all pertain to the functional application of cultivation.

That they are now described as "illnesses" is because, within the gateway of non-awakening, these four are all medicines. Now, however, we are speaking from the perspective of the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment.
To speak of it: it is fundamentally natural and does not depend on effortful application; therefore, it is merely called "sickness. As the ancient masters said:
"Cultivation is not non-existent, yet defilement must not be permitted. This means that as soon as there is the manifestation of patterns and colors, one belongs to the realm of defilement.
Therefore, to be free from these four is called purity. One who practices such contemplation contemplates the person by means of the Dharma;
it is not a contemplation of wisdom itself. That is to say, one contemplates the person who is free from affliction; such a person does not dwell in signs and possesses correct knowledge and vision.
Only such a person should be taken as a teacher and relied upon.
"Good son, those living beings in the final age who wish to practice should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to and serve virtuous friends and spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When such spiritual teachers come to approach them, they should sever arrogance; if they depart, they should sever resentment.
Regarding the manifestation of favorable and adverse conditions as being like empty space, they should realize that body and mind are ultimately equal."
All sentient beings are of one essence and without difference; by practicing in this way, one enters Perfect Enlightenment.
This answers the question of what kind of practice should be cultivated. The practice described here does not speak of the six perfections or the myriad practices;
rather, it takes as its foundation the single practice of serving spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and severing the mind of arrogance, just as in the case of the youth Sudhana.

To realize the fruit of countless kalpas of cultivation, one need only engage in the single matter of attending upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). By doing so, one immediately attains the perfection of immeasurable Dharma-gates.

This is because, by following the instructions of the spiritual friend, one does not give rise to dualistic thoughts; thus, one contemplates all circumstances—whether of union or separation, favorability or adversity—as being like empty space.
Furthermore, one realizes that one’s own body and mind are equal to those of all sentient beings. This is... [the state of non-duality].
The perception of self and others is the vessel for receiving the Way. Only through such a mind and such conduct can one correspond with the essence of the Dharma-body of Perfect Enlightenment;
thus, one is able to enter it.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age fail to attain the Way because they possess the seeds of beginningless self and other, hatred and love;
therefore, they have not yet attained liberation. If there is another person who regards an enemy as their own parent, with a mind free from duality, then all illnesses will be eliminated.
Within all phenomena, the same applies to the self and other, hatred and love.

This answer addresses the removal of what illness. The reason sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death is that they possess the seeds of beginningless ignorance, craving, and aversion, which serve as the root of the illness that obstructs the Path. Consequently, although they practice, they do not attain liberation.
Now, by serving a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and refraining from pride and resentment, one subdues these manifest [afflictions].
Practice. When one fully realizes that one’s own body and mind are equal to those of all sentient beings, then the notions of self and other cease to exist.

The seeds of attachment and aversion are naturally subdued. When one comes to regard an enemy as a friend, the seeds of attachment and aversion are severed of their own accord, and the maladies that obstruct the Path are likewise severed.
Therefore it is said: "one immediately eliminates all ailments. This is precisely the sublime medicine for eliminating disease.
"Good son, if sentient beings in the final age wish to seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), they should resolve their minds and speak these words:

'Throughout the entirety of space and for all sentient beings, I shall cause them all to enter ultimate perfect enlightenment. Within this perfect enlightenment, there shall be no one who grasps at enlightenment;
I shall eliminate all signs, including the signs of self and other. Resolving the mind in this way, one will not fall into false views."
This answers the question of what kind of mind is generated. The *Prajñā-maitreya-gāthā* states: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; its mind is non-erroneous.
This means that encompassing all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space is the vast mind.
That they all enter ultimate perfect enlightenment is the foremost mind. That within perfect enlightenment there is no one who grasps at awakening is the eternal mind. [Excluding...]
Those [notions of] self, person, and all other marks are precisely the elimination of the four ailments; they constitute the non-perverted mind.
For all practitioners, there is no essential method for receiving the Dharma from a teacher and practicing it that exceeds this. To abandon this is to fall into false views.
Therefore, it is said: "In this way, one does not fall."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"Universal Enlightenment, you should know: If sentient beings in the final age Desire to seek a virtuous friend, They should seek one who possesses right view And whose mind is far removed from the two vehicles."
This verse seeks out the teacher.
Within the Dharma, one eliminates the four illnesses, namely: effort, laxity, indifference, and cessation;
this verse relies on the Dharma to remove these illnesses.
Associate with those free from pride; remain far removed from anger and resentment.
Upon encountering various conditions, one should give rise to a sense of wonder, as if the Buddha had appeared in the world. Do not transgress the precepts of the Vinaya;
let the roots of your discipline be eternally pure.
This verse concerns the practice of not violating non-discipline (*aviniyama*).
The prose commentary states that even if the teacher appears to have faults, one must not cause sentient beings to enter into non-discipline.

Here, it is specifically said that when a disciple serves a teacher, if they observe contrary conduct, they must not follow it, lest they commit a violation of non-discipline; rather, they must ensure that their roots of precept (*śīla-mūla*) remain eternally pure.
Right Practice. The old interpretation takes this as a concluding verse for the section on "Seeking a Teacher," but that is not the original intent.

To deliver all sentient beings Ultimately to enter Perfect Enlightenment, Without the notions of self, other, person, or counterpart, And relying upon right wisdom— One will then transcend false views And realize the Nirvana of Awakening.
This verse concerns the arousal of the bodhicitta. Five lines of the verse describe the causal practices of the four types of bodhicitta; the final line reveals the realization of the fruit.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Subhūti asked regarding the majestic deportment:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, for our sakes you have extensively expounded the various skillful means of pure awakening,
so that sentient beings of the final age may attain great benefit."
We rejoice in what we have previously heard.

World-Honored One, we have now attained awakening. However, regarding those sentient beings in the future age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa who have not yet attained awakening, how should they dwell in retreat and cultivate this pure realm of *Vajracchedikā-pratyutpanna-bodhi*?
Within this *Vajracchedikā-pratyutpanna-bodhi*, there are three kinds...
"Pure Contemplation. What is its primary basis? We pray that, out of great compassion, you will bestow vast benefit upon this great assembly and the sentient beings of the final age.
To formally state the request: what is its primary basis? It is the very first expedient means.

Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again, manifesting their utmost sincerity on three occasions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family, you..."
"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means; this will bring great benefit and bestow it upon all sentient beings.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Having granted permission to speak, he exhorted them to listen.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the instruction and listened in silence,
waiting expectantly. "Good son, whether the Buddha remains in the world, after his parinirvāṇa, or during the final age of the Dharma, if there are sentient beings..."
All sentient beings who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna and believe in the Buddha’s secret Great Perfect Enlightenment Mind (*mahā-vajra-citta*), desiring to practice, should—

whether staying in a monastery or dwelling among a community during the retreat season— contemplate and examine according to their capacity as I have already explained, whenever there is a cause or circumstance for doing so.
The following is the formal response to the request. "Nature" (*gotra*) refers to one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*), which is like a faculty or capacity.

Since Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is the secret, wondrous mind, it cannot be cultivated by those who do not possess superior faculties; therefore, it is permitted that only those endowed with the Mahāyāna lineage may practice it.
The intention is that if there are no external conditions, one should remain in residence at a monastery (*vihāra*) and dwell together with the community.
If there are external conditions that prevent one from dwelling in settled concentration (*samāhita*), then one should investigate according to one's capacity.
As previously stated, one should contemplate this body and so forth.
If there are no other circumstances or causes for delay, one should immediately establish a place of practice (*maṇḍala*). One should set a time limit:
a long period of one hundred and twenty days, a medium period of one hundred days, or a short period of eighty days, and establish a pure dwelling.

This is the rule for concluding the retreat (*varṣā*). The intention is that, provided there are no external circumstances, one must prioritize the *an-gu* (summer retreat), as it facilitates entry into the Way.
The three periods may be undertaken according to one's inclination; their length originally has no fixed duration, but they are undertaken solely to advance along the Path within a set timeframe.
Furthermore, if it is during the present time, one should practice right contemplation;

if it is after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should fashion an image and, with the mind focused and the eyes fixed upon it, give rise to right mindfulness, which is equivalent to the days when the Tathāgata was still dwelling among us. One should suspend various banners and flowers for twenty-one days.
I prostrate my head before the names of all Buddhas of the ten directions. Seeking their compassion, I repent; encountering auspicious signs, my mind attains lightness and ease.
After three weeks have passed, I shall single-mindedly concentrate my mindfulness.

This is the method for observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and advancing in cultivation according to this teaching. If the Tathāgata is present in the world, one should contemplate the Buddha with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

If after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should set up an image and contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Therefore, it is said that [the practice] is identical to the eternally abiding [Buddha].
One should suspend banners and flowers extensively, as detailed in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* altar ritual; however, because the present context is extremely concise, only these points are mentioned.
Regarding the banners and flowers, "attaining a virtuous state through repentance" refers to seeing light, beholding auspicious omens, or experiencing significant dreams;

these are the signs that transgressions have been extinguished. One should focus the mind exclusively and cultivate right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), following the twenty-five wheels each with its designated markers.
To practice them in both single and combined sequences constitutes the correct application.

If, at the beginning of summer, one observes the three-month *varṣā* retreat, one should establish a pure dwelling for the sake of a bodhisattva. The mind should be detached from that of the *śrāvakas*, and there is no need for a retinue of followers.

These words describe the rules for entering the period [of retreat]. The statement regarding the bodhisattva’s dwelling is intended to distinguish it from the assemblies of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). As mentioned previously...
Regarding the term "three periods," this refers to establishing a fixed duration. To now enter the *an-guo* (rainy season retreat) is the method for entering that period.

According to the Buddhist regulations of the Western Regions, the three-month *an-guo* is collectively termed "entering summer" (*jixia*). What is here called the "beginning of summer" refers to the initial entry into that period.
According to the Vinaya regulations, at the time of entering the retreat, one must first assemble the community to perform the *poṣadha* ritual, and only thereafter enter the *an-guo*.

Regarding the many followers of the Hīnayāna: what is here called "the dwelling of a bodhisattva" means that he does not conform to those numerous groups of the Hīnayāna, but rather acts according to the personal convenience of a bodhisattva practicing contemplation within a single class of practitioners.
He need not attend to the ritual matters of the Hīnayāna *poṣadha*, nor does he require their assembly. This statement that he does not require the assembly of the Hīnayāna does not mean that he...
The preceding passage contradicts the manner of settling the assembly.
On the day of entering the *varṣā* retreat, one should stand before the Buddha and speak as follows:

"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā], so-and-so, who dwells in the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescence, enter together into the purity of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."
I take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery; my body and mind dwell in the wisdom of equanimity.

Because the self-nature of Nirvana has no attachments, I now respectfully invite you not to follow the path of the Śrāvakas, but to enter a three-month retreat together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, for the sake of cultivating the supreme cause of the Bodhisattva’s wondrous enlightenment. Do not...
"Binding the assembly.
This demonstrates the method for entering the stage of settling the mind. The previous statement that "the mind is detached from the śrāvakas" correctly shows what the bodhisattva cultivates:
namely, the practice of signless quiescence, which is not comparable to the śrāvaka’s cultivation based on attachment to signs.

"To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s monastery" means not dwelling in dependence upon the world, but rather abiding in the ground of equal quiescence where both mind and objects are forgotten.
This refers to the self-nature of Nirvana, for it is fundamentally devoid of anything—body, mind, or world—to which one could be attached.
Since this is by no means the realm of the Śrāvakas, it is said that one does not rely [upon them], but relies solely upon the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Because it is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the body, it serves as the causal condition for the sublime awakening cultivated by Bodhisattvas;
it is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-awakening and the locus of personal realization. This is a ground reached solely by Bodhisattvas;
therefore, it is said that they are not bound to a following of disciples. "So-and-so" refers to the sequence of names such as "A" or "B," which is how one should address oneself by name. Now...
When junior practitioners from various regions encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they do not state their own names, but merely say, "I am so-and-so.
This is the height of ignorance.
Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat; once the three-month period has passed, one may go wherever one wishes without hindrance.
This section indicates the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Regarding the statement "manifesting the summer retreat":

since it was previously stated that the Bodhisattva cultivates the practice of quiescence and dwells in the wisdom of the equality of nature (*samatājñāna*), why would there be a need for a fixed time limit?

Nevertheless, the reason one must necessarily take the three periods as a limit is to manifest conformity with the provisional vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, thereby inducing those who have not yet attained awakening. Once the period has passed, one may proceed according to circumstances.

Regarding "obstruction": after the precepts were established according to the interpretation of the Hīnayāna, new practitioners were required to have a companion of at least three people whenever they went out traveling, so as to prevent errors or transgressions.
Now, the Bodhisattva, through contemplation and the knowledge of settling the mind, does not necessarily require a companion;
therefore, it is said that he proceeds wherever he goes without obstruction.
Good son, if sentient beings practicing in the final age who seek the bodhisattva path enter the three periods of practice,
they must never grasp at any of the objective realms they hear of.

This demonstrates the errors and omissions [of the practitioner]. That which was "heard" refers to the twenty-five wheels of single, combined, and perfect cultivation of the three aforementioned contemplations, as well as the complete purity of each of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses; these constitute right contemplation.

As for that which was not "heard," all such realms must not be grasped, just as described in the fifty grades of the *māras* of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the [arising of]... in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Regarding the demonic activities described in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, none of them should be grasped at, for fear of falling into error.

At the beginning, there are two questions: first, concerning the summer retreat (*varṣā*); second, concerning which of the three contemplations should be taken as primary. The former [section] concludes with the answer regarding the summer retreat;
the latter provides the answer concerning the initial preparatory method (*upāya*).
"Good son, if sentient beings practice śamatha, they first grasp at ultimate stillness and do not give rise to thoughts.
When stillness reaches its peak, they become aware. Thus, this initial stillness extends from a single body to a single world; once again, it is the same for each.
Good son, if their awareness fills all worlds, then within a single world, there may be a single sentient being who gives rise to a single [thought]."
One who possesses mindfulness can know all things; it is likewise for hundreds of thousands of worlds.
Yet, none of those perceived objects ever heard by them can ultimately be grasped.
This answers the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*). First, it is the preparatory method for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

To say that one "cultivates *śamatha* by first attaining ultimate stillness" means that *śamatha* serves as the preliminary method (*pūrvaprayoga*). Regarding the term "ultimate stillness," this refers to the "cessation that realizes the truth" (*tattva-śamatha*) among the Three Cessations of the Tiantai school;
it is called "ultimate stillness" because its essence accords with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since not a single thought arises, it is [still].
A thought arises; as stillness reaches its ultimate limit, light is produced, and thus it is said that one "suddenly awakens. Regarding the phrase "initially from a single body" and so forth:
this refers to internally detaching from the body and mind while externally casting off the world, such that the internal and external are equalized in a state of tranquil immobility.
Because the body, mind, and world have been swept away into a single void, they merge with all things into a single mind, and all worlds are unified as one.
Because they belong to a single realm (*dhātu*). For all sentient beings, whenever a thought arises or a movement of mind occurs, it immediately manifests from within their own minds.
Thus, there is not a single thought that arises which is not fully known. As it is said: "When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through;

in silent illumination, it encompasses empty space. Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream. This is the pinnacle of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Only in this way...
This is called Right Contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). None of what has been heard therein should be grasped.

Good son, if sentient beings practice *samāpatti*, they should first recollect and contemplate how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, relying on various gateways, gradually practice the samādhi of diligent and arduous effort.
One extensively formulates great vows and perfumes oneself to establish the seeds; one must never again grasp at any of those perceived objects.
This demonstrates the skillful means of the provisional contemplation of *samāpatti*. The meaning of *samāpatti* corresponds to the contemplation of illusion (*māyā*).
Regarding the phrase "recalling the various practices, diligent austerities, and samādhis of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas":
this refers to contemplating how the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, while in the causal stage, practiced various difficult and painful austerities to deliver all sentient beings;
and within samādhi, they gave rise to the contemplation of illusion, personally traversing those realms with their own body and mind. Internally...
Examine the mind: various realms are experienced in their entirety as being like an illusion. By means of this contemplation of illusion, one gives rise to the vow to deliver sentient beings.

Through long-term cultivation, this becomes a seed; when it has matured over time, one is able to inwardly give rise to great compassion and pliancy, thereby initiating the sublime practices of a bodhisattva for the benefit of living beings—namely, using the contemplation of illusion to awaken illusory multitudes and acting as an illusory Buddha.
This is the matter. This refers to *samāpatti*, which takes the "illusion-like" as its primary characteristic. That which was not heard by you must ultimately not be grasped.
Good son, if sentient beings cultivate *dhyāna*, they first take the method of counting (*gaṇanā*) as their gateway; within the mind, they clearly understand the arising [of thoughts].

Abiding in the analytical discernment of the divisions and enumerations of mindfulness regarding cessation, one thus pervasively distinguishes the counts of mindfulness throughout the four modes of deportment until there is nothing not fully known.
One gradually progresses until one can know even a single drop of rain in hundreds of thousands of worlds as clearly as if seeing an object directly before the eyes.
Yet, none of those heard objects of experience can ultimately be grasped.
This demonstrates the initial method for tranquil observation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). The meaning of *dhyāna* is the single mind of the Middle Way, which is termed "tranquil observation.
To say that one first employs the method of counting refers to the very first stage of practice when entering *dhyāna*.

This is because practitioners of meditation often have minds that are excessively distracted and turbulent, making it difficult to attain stillness; therefore, they first take the method of counting as the primary means. That is to say:
First, to gather the mind: initially, return to a single breath. Relying on the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, count them from one to ten, and then from ten back to one.
Repeating this cycle, let each breath continue without interruption and each moment of mind remain clear.
Clearly distinguish every instance of arising and ceasing, progressing from a few to many, thereby testing the depth of one's concentration (*samādhi*). If practiced for a long time...
When one becomes thoroughly proficient and counts until not a single thought arises, the breath will naturally cease; the mind becomes tranquil and abides in profound stillness.

This is the mark of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When this is pervasive throughout all four postures, knowing clearly in every moment, then after a long time, hundreds of thousands of worlds are seen as manifestations of the mind alone, even to the point of clearly discerning a single drop of rain.
It is like seeing an object with one's own eyes; this is the perfection of the practice of śamatha-vipaśyanā.
As stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, those who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā do not rely on the breath; they take internal detachment from body and mind as their essential goal.

Those who rely upon the breath do so as a skillful means for beginners to collect the mind, but it is not the ultimate reliance. If one were to consider the breath as the attainment [of the goal], then...
They fall into wrong paths; this is not what they have heard.
This is called the "initial skillful means" (*upāya*) of the three contemplations.

This is the name of the concluding summary. Since the previous question asked which of the three kinds of pure contemplations should be taken as the beginning, [the text] provides the full answer and then—

This is the pointing of the finger. It is known that while the preceding twenty-five wheels only describe the contemplation of signs (*nimitta*), these three skillful means (*upāya*) constitute the very first application of effort.
This is precisely the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, where each of the twenty-five sages describes their own initial application of effort. It is this same principle.
If all sentient beings universally cultivate the three contemplations and practice with diligent vigor, this is called the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world;

this demonstrates the benefit of the three contemplations. Since these three contemplations constitute the original ground for the arising of all Tathāgatas, any being of perfect faculties who is able to universally cultivate the three contemplations is likewise called the appearance of a Tathāgata.
In this world, it is said that one ultimately achieves unimpededness. Because there is such a supreme benefit, I exhort you to practice it.
If, in the future degenerate age, sentient beings of dull faculties desire to seek the Way but fail to achieve success, it is due to the roots of their past karma.
One should diligently practice repentance and constantly give rise to hope. First, sever hatred, attachment, jealousy, and flattery;

seek the superior mind and the three kinds of pure contemplations. If one cannot achieve even one of these contemplations, one should further cultivate the others without letting the mind abandon them.
"Gradually seeking realization" refers to sentient beings of dull faculties whose hindrances are heavy; for them, it is essential to sever these hindrances through repentance (*pratikramana*).
As for "due to past karmic hindrances," these are seeds of former habitual tendencies which, at the time of current practice, are perfumed to manifest as active afflictions that obstruct the Path.

Regarding conditions: those who desire to be upright yet remain firmly entrenched in depravity, or who wish to be pure yet are biased toward defilement, are driven by their long-standing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, one must diligently practice repentance to eliminate the obstacles of past karma. Once these karmic obstacles are eliminated, the conditions for the Way can be fulfilled.
As for "constantly giving rise to hope," this refers to the aspiration and vow to sever karmic obstacles. Thus, it is said immediately below:
First, one must sever hatred, attachment, and so forth—namely, greed, anger, and delusion—as well as the conceit of a superior mind (*abhimāna*).

This means that once the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are severed and their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) no longer arise, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) can be eliminated and the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) will easily be accomplished.

If this contemplation cannot be attained, one must again cultivate that [specific] contemplation; this is the intended meaning of the "twenty-five wheels" (*pañcaviṃśati-cakra*). Therefore, it is said: "gradually."
Next, the request for realization.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: All sentient beings Who seek the unsurpassed path..."
First, one should establish a three-period retreat to repent for karmic actions from beginningless time; after passing seven times three days, one then engages in right contemplation.
That which is not the realm of what has been heard cannot ultimately be grasped;
through the ultimate stillness of *śamatha* and the correct mindfulness of *samādhi*, this is the gateway to the enumeration of the dhyānas.
This is called the threefold pure contemplation; if one can diligently practice it, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
For those of dull faculties who have not yet attained accomplishment, they should always repent with a diligent mind.
When all sins and obstacles from beginningless time are extinguished, the realm of the Buddha will then manifest before them.
The section on the Correct Teaching (Zhengzongfen) concludes above.

Below follows the section on the Dissemination of the Teaching (Liutongfen). Thereupon, Bodhisattva Xianshou rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Subhūti further inquired regarding the majestic deportment:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have extensively expounded for us and for the sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age, awakening us to the inconceivable matters of the Tathāgata.
We rejoice in the great meaning of the entire sūtra as we have heard it previously."
Now he formally sets forth his request:
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this Mahāyāna teaching? How should it be upheld? What merit do sentient beings obtain by practicing it?
And how may I protect those who uphold this scripture and cause this teaching to spread until it reaches its ultimate destination?"
This inquiry concerns the title of the sutra and the dissemination of this Dharma. There are five such inquiries: first, the inquiry regarding the title of the sutra;

second, the inquiry regarding its reverent upholding; third, the inquiry regarding its merit; fourth, the inquiry regarding its protection and maintenance; and fifth, the inquiry as to what stage of attainment the dissemination reaches.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again, manifesting his utmost sincerity three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."
You are now able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the merits and names of such scriptural teachings as these.
Listen attentively now; I shall explain them for you.
Having granted permission for the discourse and requested that they listen attentively,
the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, together with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence,
waiting expectantly.
Good son, this sutra has been spoken by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, is the refuge of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

This is a general praise of the excellence of the Dharma, intended to inspire faith and reverence. This sutra is the fundamental practice for attaining the stage of the ground of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
it is that which has been spoken by all Buddhas, guarded by the Tathāgatas, and taught to Bodhisattvas, serving as the refuge for Bodhisattvas.
It flows forth from all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, and *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is the eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
This sutra is titled *The Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Dhāraṇī*; it is also titled *The Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*;
it is also titled *The King of Secret Samādhis*; it is also titled *The Determinate Realm of the Tathāgata*; and it is also titled *The Self-Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha*.
"Differentiation. You should uphold this.
This response regarding names indicates that there are five types of titles for a sutra. In the present compilation of the scripture's title, only two of these remain.

The traditional interpretation of the five names categorizes them according to teaching, principle, and practice: *Sūtra* refers to the teaching; *Guhyarāja-samādhi* [refers to the principle];... [and so forth].

This is explained in terms of practice; all others are explained in terms of principle. Because it is the single mind of the Middle Way, it is called "esoteric" (*guhya*); it does not refer to "esoteric speech.
Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, the various distinctions are established. The meaning is exhausted here; one should uphold it in this manner.
"Good son, this sutra reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, can fully proclaim it.
If Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this to practice, they will gradually advance until they reach the stage of Buddhahood."
This praises the supremacy of the Dharma, intending to encourage its cultivation. To answer the question of "reaching what stage":

from the moment every Buddha attains enlightenment, they all take Perfect Enlightenment as their fundamental cause; and when they become Buddhas to benefit sentient beings, they likewise teach only this Dharma to instruct Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, because there is no other dharma besides this, I exhort you to practice it so that you may reach the stage of Buddhahood.
Good son, this sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna. Sentient beings with sudden capacities awaken through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice gradually.
It is like the great ocean, which does not reject even small streams, down to those as tiny as mosquitoes and gnats.
Asuras who drink its water all attain full satisfaction. What merit does this answer possess?

It is because it alone is intended for those of superior faculties; thus the teaching is called "Perfect and Sudden. Because it universally encompasses those of the three faculties, its merit is greatest.
This is because it is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings, through which all realize Perfect Awakening.
Therefore, there is nothing that is not fully satisfied. It is like the great ocean, which does not refuse even small streams; whether large or small, all who drink from it are satisfied.
Good son, suppose there were someone who filled the entire trichiliocosm with pure seven-jeweled treasures. With these...
To practice giving is not as meritorious as for someone to hear the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning.

This comparison reveals its superiority: while worldly treasures filling a world-system merely provide for that which is outflowing (āsrava), a single word of the ultimate truth can surely transform an ordinary person into a sage;
therefore, the merit [of the latter] exceeds [the former] by a factor of ten thousandfold.
Good son, suppose there were someone who taught as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers so that they attained the fruit of Arhatship;
this would not equal the merit of someone who proclaims and analyzes even half a verse of this sutra.
This compares humans to the Dharma to further manifest its benefit. Although small fruits may be numerous, they ultimately lack actual realization.
This half-verse of the sutra is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is difficult to compare.
"Good son, if there is anyone who hears the name of this sutra and their faith is not confused,

you should know that such a person has planted roots of merit and wisdom not under one or two Buddhas alone, but has planted various roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, having heard the teachings of this sutra."
This praises the superior capacity for receptivity; that is to say, those who are able to believe and accept this Dharma must have extensively cultivated merit and wisdom under many Buddhas.
It is certainly not something that can be endured by those of meager merit and thin virtue.
"O son of good family, you should protect those practitioners in the final age, ensuring that evil Māras and various heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies and minds,
causing them to fall into despondency and retreat."
This is the formal entrustment for the propagation [of the teaching]. It is considered the foremost priority because it protects the practitioner.
For those who cultivate this Dharma, their very life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) is at stake; if they are disturbed by evil Māras and give rise to regression, their life of wisdom will be severed.
Therefore, one must protect and uphold it.
At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty thousand *vajras*, including Agnīśikha-vajra, Vajravidāraṇa, Nīlambava-vajra, and others, together with their retinues.
They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if in the future final age there are any sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Great [Dharma]..."

We shall protect you as we would our own eyes. From this place until the site of your attainment of enlightenment, we, the Vajras, leading our own retinues, shall guard you morning and evening so that you do not regress. In your home, may there never be calamities or obstacles;
may pestilence be extinguished; and may wealth and treasures abound, never lacking at any time.
This passage describes the Vajra’s reception of the entrustment and his vow to protect those who uphold this sutra.
As for "Vajra," it is so named because the Dharma-protecting deity wields this precious vajra; furthermore, the precious vajra is capable of shattering all things.
Regarding the term "Fire-Head Vajra" (Huǒshǒu Jīngāng): this refers to one who has flames upon the head.

This is what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by the transformation of a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom; it is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva. As for "Nīlambā," its translation is not yet known.
It is said that these deities are all those who, through their long-standing practice, made vows to protect the Dharma; therefore, they are constantly present at the Buddha’s assemblies.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, the twenty-eight celestial kings, Sumeru the King of Mountains, the Heavenly Kings who Protect the Nation, and others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I...”
They shall also protect those who uphold this sutra, constantly ensuring they remain at peace and their resolve never regresses.
This passage describes how the various devas receive the entrustment to protect and uphold the sutra. Mahābrahmā is the king of the first dhyāna heaven.
He serves as the lord of the Sahā world. Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, this king acts as the host for the invitation.

As for the twenty-eight heavens, these collectively comprise all the devas of the triple world: namely, the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the eighteen heavens of the dhyāna realms, and the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Mount Sumeru is singled out, and Śakra is specifically mentioned as its ruler; he is the lord of the desire realm. The Heavenly Kings who protect the nation belong to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*).
As the lords who protect the boundaries of the realm, they intend that all the devas of the three realms shall likewise protect the Dharma.

At that time, a powerful king of ghosts named Kumbhāṇḍa, together with one hundred thousand kings of ghosts, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we too shall protect this dhāraṇī.”
I shall have people attend to him morning and evening, ensuring he does not retreat or yield.
Within a distance of one yojana of his dwelling, if there are any ghosts or spirits who invade his domain, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.
This passage describes the spirits and deities who have received the entrustment to protect and uphold this sutra. Kumbhāṇḍa is also called Guhyapāda; it is translated here as the "Terrifying Ghost.
It feeds on the vital essence of humans and moves as swiftly as the wind. Its transformations are boundless, and it dwells in forests and wilds presiding over the hosts of ghosts;
therefore, it is titled "King. It does not belong to the realms of humans or devas, but resides alone in the ghost realm (*preta-gati*). This...
Once the spirits have made their vow to provide protection, no evil spirits whatsoever will be able to cause harm.
A *yojana* is forty *li*; this means that within a protected area of forty *li*, there shall be no calamities.

Question: This sutra was spoken by the Buddha while he resided within the Great Radiance Treasury (Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha) and entered into samādhi, for the sake of a certain class of great bodhisattvas on earth.
Since it is beyond the reach of those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), they were not listed in the previous assembly.
Furthermore, how could there be devas and spirits who made vows to protect it? Answer: This is not something that ordinary intellect can fathom. Nevertheless...

The Buddha abides in the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*). In meaning, this corresponds to the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsa-śānti-kṣetra*), wherein self and other are equal, and both speaker and listener are non-existent.

Since it is said that "within the realm of non-duality, all pure lands are manifested," this includes not only the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*) but necessarily encompasses the Land of Common Residence (*saha-loka*).

This is because the Land of True Reward within the Flower Bank World (*padma-garbha-loka*) necessarily subsumes the Land of Common Residence. Thus, at the Dharma assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the various devas...
The divine kings each praised the Buddha and each attained a distinct Dharma-gate; how could it be that they were entirely excluded?
Therefore, from the perspective of the Dharma, the two vehicles have no share in this; yet from the perspective of the objective realm, both ordinary beings and sages are universally encompassed.

Moreover, as the perfect voice resounds far and wide, instantly pervading ten lands—how could the various heavenly kings of this world not look up to such a sublime assembly? Furthermore, as for the reflected images...
This manifestation as an echo dwells within the realm of the Buddhas; there is no room for doubt.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of attendants, as well as the kings of the gods, the Brahma kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy, and they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

This is the concluding summary. According to the ancient interpretation, these eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and so forth—must have internally realized the dharma-nature and manifested in these forms;

however, they are not listed at the beginning of the assembly. This implies that the Dharma is supreme. Since the concluding summary encompasses the entire multitude, it follows by implication that they all heard [the teaching] together.
Therefore, all were greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
*The Direct Explanation of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Lower (End).
Postscript following the carving of the commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
The Dharmakāya transmigrates through the five paths of rebirth and is called "sentient beings. This is the ground of pure awakening for sentient beings;
it is the very ground upon which all Buddhas originally set out. Yet, because they are obscured by ignorance, they do not realize it despite using it daily.

Therefore, our World-Honored One has exerted himself to specially manifest within the triple world, condescending to the capacities of all beings to point out the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by each individual.
Sentient beings have been deluded for a long time; their ignorance is profound and their obscurations are deep. Without contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), there is no way to penetrate them.

Therefore, the wondrous gate of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is established as the essential means for awakening the mind. This is truly because those with dull faculties are unable to practice all aspects simultaneously;

thus, throughout the teachings of the one lifetime [of the Buddha], the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) was taught first to destroy the afflictions of views and craving, followed by the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
One contemplates [the phenomenal] to shatter the sands of delusion; subsequently, one speaks of the Middle Way Contemplation (*madhyamaka*) to shatter ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, because the sequential and distinct stages of practice cannot lead to the perfect realization of the One Mind, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is taught to encompass the three contemplations, perfectly illuminating the One Mind and instantaneously shattering ignorance.
This constitutes the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate. Nevertheless, its text encompasses the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), and its teachings...
It encompasses the five periods, the ten realms of both sages and ordinary beings, and the entirety of delusion and enlightenment, cause and effect, in exhaustive detail.

Yet, students of shallow wisdom and coarse minds find the text vast and its meaning profound, making it difficult to penetrate due to its obscurity; how much more so for those who seek to transcend words to grasp the meaning and wondrously accord with the One Mind?
As for that which is most simple yet refined, most pertinent yet essential, nothing surpasses it.

This is the most supreme Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). Its text comprises no more than thirteen thousand words, yet it comprehensively encompasses the boundless ocean of teachings and subsumes the Perfect School of the Dharma-realm.
It penetrates the source of the One Mind and traverses the principles of the Three Contemplations.
The alternation of the partial and the correct; the singular, the manifold, and the perfect cultivation; the exhaustive investigation of the false ruler;

and the excision of the maladies of Chan—through these, one awakens to the wondrous gate of the mind and enters directly by a single leap. This is what is called the true scripture of the Dharma-realm and the sublime practice for attaining Buddhahood.

Sudden awakening and sudden realization are like viewing fruit in the palm of one’s hand; this is the secret, wondrous meaning of the direct pointing transmitted from the West. Beyond this, there is nothing further to be contained.
Indeed, among all those who study Buddhism, there are none who do not take this as their guide. In the past, Master Guifeng composed a brief commentary (*lüeshu*), which seems too concise;
he also wrote a separate sub-commentary (*xiaochao*), which is perhaps too prolix. However, where the text encounters resistance, the meaning fails to be fully conveyed;

when the meaning is not fully conveyed, the contemplation of principle (*liguan*) cannot be clarified; and when the contemplation of principle is not clarified, one becomes dazed and lost at the crossroads.
Yet there is no fixed destination [for them]. While dwelling in the mountains in the leisure between meditation sessions, I occasionally unrolled this scroll and felt deep regret.

Thereupon, I commented upon the meaning of the Patriarch’s sub-commentary to provide a direct access to the sutra text. Valuing the realization of the Buddha’s intent rather than the mere words and phrases, I have composed this "Direct Explanation" (Zhijie) to establish a karmic connection with the Dharma.
It was roughly completed when I happened to meet the layman from Xin’an, Master Cheng Mengyang, whose courtesy name is Juewo.
Upon hearing this, they were filled with joy and reverence. Consequently, the layman Wu Qigao specially requested that it be carved into printing blocks. I, therefore, sighed and said:
"The Buddha taught that upholding even a single four-line verse brings greater merit than bestowing the seven treasures upon as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.

This is because treasures are causes for outflowing (sāsrava) existence, whereas the Dharma is the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood; the difference between them is like that between heaven and an abyss. This is what our Buddha praised with his own golden mouth."
The merit bestowed by Master Cheng’s gift is immeasurable; it shall be equal to empty space. I respectfully inscribe this at the end so that those who observe may know its origin. At this time...
Postscript to the Direct Explanation of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment,
composed by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇa Hanshan Shi Deqing of Zhongxing Caoxi,
on the full moon day of the second month of summer in the year of Renxu, the second year of the Tianqi reign.

Originally, when Fuxi drew his trigrams and Wenwang appended his explanations, the Sages relied upon these to set forth their words. When Kumārajīva translated and Dao’an studied, the Indian masters thereby expanded the teachings.
Were it not for those who give rise to wisdom and knowledge, one could not inquire into or seek after them through drilling and probing. A summer insect cannot be spoken of ice;

only a firefly’s light can illuminate the night. Since the Han dynasty summoned the dream of the jade maiden and the flowers, and the Hu images were brought over, the eight tones and nine divisions of scripture have vied with one another in abundance.

The five vehicles, the four analytical knowledges, and the three emptinesses—herein, the transmission of teachings does not conform to a single, uniform thread. Those who enter by looking toward the gate always find their brows hanging down in dejection;

those who seek to ascend by following the shore find their steps faltering. Although the clouds of compassion provide universal shade and the rain of Dharma falls incessantly, [the seekers remain hindered].
Those who are able to borrow its sprinkling and moistening to deepen their hearts, or to look up to its pervasive coverage and transcend their spirits, are truly rare indeed.

As for the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, it is especially the wondrous truth of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. What is perfected in "perfection"? What is awakened in "enlightenment"? How ultimate it is!
Who could possibly conceive of it through thought? Only the Chan Master Guifeng of the Tang Dynasty fully understood its essential purpose and refined it with precision.
This commentary may be said to stand alone like a raised banner, directly upholding the teachings of both past and present.
Yet, as for the flowers in a mirror or the moon in water, how could they ever possess fixed shadows or fixed forms?

Just as fine jade and dull gold do not hinder being carved and recast again and again, there appeared the Great Master Hanshan of Mount Kuanglu, whose noble bearing and towering stature possessed the elegance of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; he purified his thoughts and washed away his passions.
He drew forth the waters of Lake Anavatapta; with fierce vigor and diligence, he donned the armor of practice; his precepts were as pure and translucent as a lustrous pearl.
Once having launched the vessel of wisdom, he traveled long upon the ocean of enlightenment. Bamboo slips and silk volumes appeared as if from opened tombs;

those crumbling against walls were all harmoniously integrated. Jade seals and golden caskets emerged from the earth; granular treasuries were all thoroughly soaked and nourished. He held fast to these for many years.
Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) penetrates its all-encompassing scope; the mission of the West’s arrival exhausts inquiry and realization. This supreme, perfect, and numinous state is elucidated:

its phrases are detailed and analyzed, its principles are interwoven and linked. Beyond the refinement of the new and the cleansing of the old, the brilliance of the brush follows the precious flowers as they fall together.

At the moment when seals meet and symbols coincide, the leaves of the text display their fragrance equal to the *palm-leaf* manuscripts (*pattra*). Both the manifest and the hidden are fully revealed, and the radiant light shines forth in transcendent clarity.
The Dragon Palace suddenly loses its depth; how could Vulture Peak be said to be steep? It is because the True Source and the Real Aspect have long accompanied him in the *paryaṅka* posture;
thus he stands tall as doors and windows are opened. His views and insights are beyond the ordinary; as he sits upon his seat waving the fly-whisk, he expounds his discourse and unfolds its meaning.
It flows profusely like the brackish waters of the Ganges, and its resonance is deep, like a great bell awaiting a strike. Now, at this time—

Using silver in place of metal, it serves as a *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk). It carves through the undifferentiated primordial chaos (*hongmeng*) and gathers what was attained by the "elephant-net" (*xiangwang*).
Thus, the compassionate countenances of the Buddhas are made to manifest joy once more, and the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) of the two groups of six together assume their majestic deportment.

Indeed, those who awakened first and those who awakened later alike possess the Dharma-eye; whether this teaching or that teaching, they all open the gate of Chan. Furthermore, the Weaver Maiden and the Sea-Woman...
People need not possess identical capacities to weave together strings of mani-jewels; these may truly be treasured side by side in the same casket. Guifeng was peerless, and Hanshan was singular.
As for Yang, my faculties are ordinary and lack brilliance, and my vessel is dull and prone to melting away. Gazing toward the Bridge of Dharma, I know how to hasten with uplifted feet;

yet facing the Treasury of Sutras, I am like one staring at a blank wall, unable to see. Now, holding this collection of commentaries, I have encountered what I had never heard before. It is my humble thought that...
Master Han’s compassionate heart was most fervent; his Buddha-vow was fully realized as he specifically entrusted these pomegranates and jujubes so that they might be widely disseminated.

Furthermore, tracing back to Master Han, we see that throughout kalpas of calamities and hardships, he relied on the Way for refinement. His karma was not something that could be obstructed by the pushing of mountains;

rather, he naturally neutralized danger through the power of the intoxicated elephant. May the assembly, in upholding and transmitting this, add the silent realization of his flourishing protection and compassion.
By partaking of the nectar of immortality, one dissolves the frost of delusion; by attending to the torch of wisdom, one treads the path of enlightenment.

Thus, the person does not fail the Master’s intent, and the Master may repay the Buddha’s kindness. In total, [this work consists of] several fascicles, compiled into a single volume, titled *The Direct Explanation of Perfect Enlightenment*.
As for other commentaries on Confucian texts and Buddhist scriptures that have already circulated in the world, they are too numerous to enumerate in detail.

Fortunately, as the precious wheel of the Dharma constantly turns, one need not labor to distinguish its sound with a golden bell. If this were merely called "Zen of words," then who in the world would praise the wisdom of silent seclusion?
Out of reverence, I have sought to offer praise and, though it may be presumptuous, have ventured to propagate it.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Renxu year of the Ming Tianqi era by Cheng Mengyang, Inner Historian of Xin’an, in reverent salutation.
